abstract:
Author(s): Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, and Aleksey K. Fedorov

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021003] Published Tue Jun 03, 2025.

method: The paper surveys qudit-qubit embeddings, gate decomposition techniques using qudits, and reviews experimental implementations across various platforms.
result: Qudits can reduce gate counts and circuit depth for multiqubit gates, with experimental demonstrations in trapped ions, superconducting circuits, and photonics.
conclusion: Qudits are a promising resource for quantum computing, especially for native multilevel operations, though challenges in control and coherence remain.

title: On The Addressability Problem On Css Codes
authors: Jérôme Guyot And Samuel Jaques
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2145 (2026).

Recent discoveries in asymptotically good quantum codes have intensified research on their application in quantum computation and fault-tolerant operations. This study focuses on the addressability problem within CSS codes: we ask what circuits might implement logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits. With some notion of fault-tolerance, we prove several impossibility results: for CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address a logical [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], or [MATH] to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using a circuit made only from 1-local Clifford gates. Furthermore, we show that one cannot permute the logical qubits in a code purely by permuting the physical qubits, if the rate of the code is (asymptotically) greater than 1/3 and the distance is at least 3. We can show a similar no-go result for [MATH]s and [MATH]s between two such high-rate codes, albeit under a more restrictive assumption on the circuit, which we call "global" (though recent addressable CCZ gates use global circuits). This work pioneers the study of distance-preserving addressability in quantum codes, mainly by considering automorphisms of the code. This perspective offers new insights and potential directions for future research. We argue that studying this trade off between addressability and efficiency of the codes is essential to understand better how to do efficient quantum computation.

.
tldr: This paper proves impossibility results for addressing logical qubits in high-rate CSS codes using local Clifford circuits, and shows that permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is limited by code rate.
motivation: Understanding how to implement logical gates on subsets of logical qubits is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, especially with asymptotically good codes.
method: The authors use automorphism theory of CSS codes and combinatorial arguments to derive no-go theorems for addressability under local Clifford circuits and physical permutations.
result: For CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address logical X, Z, H, or S gates to a strict subset of logical qubits using 1-local Clifford circuits. Also, permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is impossible if the rate exceeds 1/3 and distance ≥ 3.
conclusion: There is a fundamental trade-off between addressability and code efficiency, which must be considered for practical quantum computation.

title: Long-time Freeness In The Kicked Top
authors: Elisa Vallini And Silvia Pappalardi
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2129 (2026).

Recent work highlighted the importance of higher-order correlations in quantum dynamics for a deeper understanding of quantum chaos and thermalization. The full Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis, the framework encompassing correlations, can be formalized using the language of Free Probability theory. In this context, chaotic dynamics at long times are proposed to lead to free independence or "freeness" of observables. In this work, we investigate these issues in a paradigmatic semiclassical model – the kicked top – which exhibits a transition from integrability to chaos. Despite its simplicity, we identify several non-trivial features. By numerically studying 2n-point out-of-time-order correlators, we show that in the fully chaotic regime, long-time freeness is reached exponentially fast. These considerations lead us to introduce a large deviation theory for freeness that enables us to define and analyze the associated time scale. The numerical results confirm the existence of a hierarchy of different time scales, indicating a multifractal approach to freeness in this model. Our findings provide novel insights into the long-time behavior of chaotic dynamics and may have broader implications for the study of many-body quantum dynamics.

.
tldr: This paper studies the approach to freeness in the kicked top model, revealing a multifractal hierarchy of time scales for higher-order correlations in chaotic quantum dynamics.
motivation: Understanding higher-order correlations in quantum dynamics is crucial for a deeper theory of quantum chaos and thermalization, and free probability provides a framework to describe the long-time behavior of observables.
method: The authors numerically compute 2n-point out-of-time-order correlators in the kicked top model across integrable and chaotic regimes, and introduce a large deviation theory for freeness to analyze the associated time scales.
result: In the fully chaotic regime, long-time freeness is reached exponentially fast, and the analysis reveals a hierarchy of different time scales indicating a multifractal approach to freeness.
conclusion: The findings provide novel insights into the long-time behavior of chaotic dynamics and may have broader implications for many-body quantum dynamics, particularly in the context of thermalization and the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis.

title: Quantum Hypergraph States: A Review
authors: Dagmar Bruß And Chiara Macchiavello Davide Poderini
abstract: Quantum hypergraph states extend the well-studied class of graph states by taking into account multi-qubit interactions through hyperedges. They provide a powerful framework to represent a family of quantum states with genuine multipartite entanglement. In this review, we provide a compact overview of the formal structure, entanglement characteristics, and operational relevance of hypergraph states in quantum information theory. We begin by introducing their mathematical foundations and generalizations of the stabilizer formalism. A central focus is placed on their entanglement properties, including the classification under local unitary and stochastic local operations with classical communication, the quantification of multipartite entanglement, and detection techniques via entanglement witnesses. We also explore other nonclassical features of hypergraph states, such as contextuality and genuine multipartite nonlocality, derived from stabilizer-based Bell-type inequalities. Additional attention is given to the role of hypergraph states in error correction, and as a computational resource in measurement-based quantum computation, and to their non-stabilizer character, quantified via resource-theoretic measures of quantum magic. Finally we review their generalization to higher dimensions, i.e. to qudits and continuous variables.
tldr: A comprehensive review of quantum hypergraph states, covering their mathematical structure, entanglement properties, nonclassical features, and applications in quantum information.
motivation: Hypergraph states generalize graph states to multi-qubit interactions, offering a richer framework for studying multipartite entanglement and quantum information protocols.
method: The paper reviews the stabilizer formalism for hypergraph states, entanglement classification under LU and SLOCC, entanglement quantification and detection, contextuality and nonlocality, error correction, measurement-based quantum computation, and resource theories of magic.
result: It provides a unified overview of hypergraph states, highlighting their genuine multipartite entanglement, non-stabilizer character, and operational roles in quantum computing and communication.
conclusion: Hypergraph states are a versatile tool in quantum information theory, with potential for advancing entanglement theory, quantum computation, and quantum foundations.

title: Robust Negativity In The Quantum-to-classical Transition Of Kerr Dynamics
authors: Mohsin Raza, John B. Debrota, Ariel Shlosberg, Noah Lordi, And Ivan H. Deutsch
abstract:
Author(s): Mohsin Raza, John B. DeBrota, Ariel Shlosberg, Noah Lordi, and Ivan H. Deutsch

We establish three timescales that govern the dynamics, each with distinct characteristics. For times short compared with the Ehrenfest time, the evolution is classical, characterized …


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 013708] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper quantifies the quantum-to-classical transition in Kerr nonlinear dynamics under loss, identifying three distinct timescales and showing that negativity in the Wigner function is robust to moderate loss.
motivation: Understanding the quantum-to-classical transition is fundamental to quantum optics and quantum information. The Kerr nonlinearity is a key resource for generating nonclassical states, but its fragility under decoherence is not fully characterized.
method: The authors analyze the single-mode Kerr Hamiltonian with photon loss using a master equation approach. They derive analytical expressions for the Wigner function negativity and identify three timescales: Ehrenfest time, collapse time, and revival time.

conclusion: The robustness of negativity suggests that Kerr dynamics can still generate useful nonclassical states for quantum information processing even in the presence of realistic loss.

motivation: Manual design of quantum circuits is challenging and hardware noise degrades performance; automated search can optimize circuits for specific tasks and noise models.
method: The framework integrates a noise model into the training of variational quantum circuits and employs a nondominated sorting genetic algorithm to explore the architecture space.
result: The proposed method yields quantum circuits with improved fidelity and task performance compared to baseline architectures under noisy conditions.
conclusion: Noise-aware architecture search is effective for automating the design of robust quantum circuits, advancing practical quantum computing.

title: Stationary Two-qubit Entanglement Mediated By One-dimensional Plasmonic Nanoarrays

abstract:

Entanglement is one of the key measures of quantum correlations present in nanophotonic systems, with promising applications in quantum optics and beyond. Authors of previous studies have shown that the degree of entanglement between two quantum dot (QD) qubits is preserved when a metal nanoparticle…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 065410] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies stationary entanglement between two quantum dot qubits mediated by one-dimensional plasmonic nanoarrays.
motivation: Understanding and preserving entanglement in nanophotonic systems is crucial for quantum information processing, but decoherence from plasmonic losses poses a challenge.
method: The authors model two quantum dots coupled to a plasmonic waveguide array and solve for the steady-state entanglement using master equation techniques.
result: They find that stationary entanglement can be achieved and controlled by tuning the qubit separation and the array parameters, with robustness against certain losses.
conclusion: Plasmonic nanoarrays provide a viable platform for generating and maintaining entanglement between distant qubits, with potential applications in quantum networks.

[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033043] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: A protocol for verifiable delegated variational quantum algorithms using trap qubits and classical verification.
motivation: Small-scale users face hardware constraints when executing quantum operations, making it desirable to delegate computations to powerful quantum servers while maintaining verifiability.
method: The protocol combines variational quantum algorithms with trap-based verification techniques, where the client inserts trap qubits and checks their outcomes to detect malicious behavior.

title: Efficient Quantum-Enhanced Classical Simulation For Patches Of Quantum Landscapes

motivation: Simulating quantum circuits classically is hard, but for small patches of the landscape, efficient surrogates may exist, enabling hybrid quantum-classical optimization.

title: Exploring Imaginary Coordinates: Disparity In The Shape Of Quantum State Space In Even And Odd Dimensions
authors: Simon Morelli, Santiago Llorens, And Jens Siewert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2153 (2026).

The state of a finite-dimensional quantum system is described by a density matrix that can be decomposed into a real diagonal, a real off-diagonal and and an imaginary off-diagonal part. The latter plays a peculiar role. While it is intuitively clear that some of the imaginary coordinates cannot have the same extension as their real counterparts the precise relation is not obvious. We give a complete characterization of the constraints in terms of tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates. Our description entails a three-dimensional Bloch ball-type model for the state space. We uncover a surprising qualitative difference for the state-space boundaries in even and odd dimensions.

.
tldr: This paper fully characterizes the constraints on imaginary Bloch coordinates for finite-dimensional quantum states, revealing a parity-dependent shape of the state space.
motivation: Understanding the geometry of quantum state space is fundamental to quantum information theory, and the role of imaginary coordinates was not fully characterized.
method: The authors derive tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates, constructing a three-dimensional Bloch ball model that captures the state space boundaries.
result: They find a surprising qualitative difference in the state-space boundaries between even and odd dimensions, with the imaginary coordinates having different constraints.
conclusion: The work provides a complete geometric picture of the state space, which may have implications for entanglement detection and quantum state tomography.

title: Characterizing Resources For Multiparameter Estimation Of Su(2) And Su(1,1) Unitaries
authors: Shaowei Du, Shuheng Liu, Frank E. S. Steinhoff, And Giuseppe Vitagliano
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2130 (2026).

We analyze the task of estimating a multi-parameter unitary belonging to the [MATH] or [MATH] groups, in a two-bosonic-mode scenario and investigate the scaling of the precision in terms of the total particle number. For the [MATH] case, the total particle number is conserved by the evolution and we discuss optimal states in fixed-[MATH] subspaces, identifying eigenstates of [MATH] as useful resources, even allowing simultaneous Heisenberg precision scaling for all three parameters. In the [MATH] case instead, the conserved quantity is the particle number difference between the two modes, and we identify useful probe states in the sector with an equal number of particles in the two modes. These states are analogous to the [MATH] case and would also allow simultaneous Heisenberg precision scaling for all three parameters. We then consider the more pragmatic scenario of an estimation via expectation values of time-evolved observables, which we restrict to be the first two moments of the generators. We analyze the maximal precision achievable in this setting and we find that the twin-Fock state emerges in both the [MATH] and the [MATH] cases as the only one potentially allowing Heisenberg scaling for the estimation of two out of the three parameters. As a complement, we also consider other probe states with fluctuating number of particles, with measurements restricted to quadratic expressions in the mode operators. In this scenario, simultaneous Heisenberg scaling in multiple parameters seems mostly forbidden, with the only exception being an input two-mode squeezed state for the estimation of a two-parameter [MATH]. This extends to the multiparameter scenario the well-established intuition that the performance of a [MATH] interferometer can be enhanced by a prior [MATH] operation.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes resources for multiparameter estimation of SU(2) and SU(1,1) unitaries in a two-bosonic-mode scenario, identifying optimal probe states and precision scaling.
motivation: Multiparameter estimation is crucial for quantum metrology, and understanding the resources that enable Heisenberg scaling for multiple parameters simultaneously is an open problem.
method: The authors analyze the precision scaling in terms of total particle number for SU(2) and SU(1,1) unitaries, considering both optimal states in fixed-number subspaces and practical measurements restricted to first two moments of generators.
result: Eigenstates of J_z for SU(2) and twin-Fock states for both groups allow simultaneous Heisenberg scaling for all three parameters; with restricted measurements, twin-Fock states enable Heisenberg scaling for two parameters, while two-mode squeezed states allow it for a two-parameter SU(1,1) estimation.
conclusion: The work extends the intuition that prior SU(1,1) operations can enhance interferometer performance to the multiparameter scenario, providing guidance for experimental quantum metrology.

title: Classically Realizable Incompatibility
authors: Songyi Liu, Yongjun Wang, Baoshan Wang, Yunyi Jia, Chang He
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Incompatibility constitutes a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics. However, not every quantum observable non-classical property arises from incompatibility, nor can all quantum scenarios be fully captured by incompatibility alone. Within the framework of partial Boolean algebra (pBA), we research the structural properties of incompatibility scenarios. We introduce a unified method to realize any incompatibility scenario via a classical game, and the construction is extendable to any scenario embeddable into a Boolean algebra. The exclusivity graph offers a precise characterization of incompatibility scenarios. We prove that every exclusivity graph is the atom graph of an exclusive pBA, which is embedded into a Boolean algebra. These results provide a necessary condition for exclusivity graphs and a sufficient condition for atom graphs.

result: They provide a necessary condition for exclusivity graphs and a sufficient condition for atom graphs, establishing a precise characterization of incompatibility scenarios.
conclusion: The results offer a classical realization of quantum incompatibility and deepen the understanding of the structure of incompatibility, though the contribution is more foundational than directly applicable to core quantum information topics.

title: Quantum Scattering Model Of Dual Parallel Mach Zehnder Electro Optic Modulators: General Formalism, Impairments, And Applications To Frequency-Bin Photonic Quantum States
authors: Mar Yuste, Carlos R. Fern\'andez Pousa, Javier Fraile Pel\'aez, Jos\'e Capmany
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a quantum mechanical model of dual parallel Mach Zehnder electro-optic modulators (DPMZMs), derived using the quantum scattering formalism [1,2]. We obtain the complete, unrestricted transformation of single-photon and coherent input states through the DPMZM architecture, including independent radiofrequency drive conditions on each internal modulator, and recover the symmetric push pull operating point as an exact special case. We numerically evaluate the resulting frequency comb structure, quantify the device sensitivity to bias error, modulation-index imbalance, and RF noise, and use the model to design a DP-MZM-based frequency-bin qubit source, reporting its fidelity as a function of these impairments.

conclusion: The model enables design and optimization of frequency-bin qubit sources for quantum networks, with quantified trade-offs due to impairments.

title: Benchmarking Error Mitigation: Artefactual Improvements In Zero-Noise Extrapolation
authors: Wolfgang Mauerer Dominik K\"oster
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable benchmarking of Quantum Error Mitigation (QEM) requires distinguishing genuine improvements from artefacts of the post-processing arithmetic. In this paper, we expose a failure mode in Richardson Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE), a widely used technique routinely (and often implicitly) relied upon in benchmarks and experiments. When noise amplification operates beyond usable signals - a regime that is quickly reached on current hardware for non-trivial circuits - we show that the extrapolation no longer reflects the underlying physics, but collapses into a fixed rescaling of a single noisy measurement, producing a bogus apparent improvement that is independent of noise amplification. This poses a rarely considered threat to the validity of many empirical evaluations in quantum computing. Measurements on real hardware (IQM Euro-Q-Exa) confirm this collapse with ordinary folding alone: as circuit depth erodes the signal, the reported estimate decouples from the truth and overshoots the ideal by up to 21%. We further introduce a matched-cost "garbage-folding" negative control that carries no usable signal yet reports a larger apparent improvement than genuine folding - showing that the magnitude of an improvement is not evidence of its correctness - alongside a zero-cost check flagging the artefact from data a benchmark already holds. We distil both into a short reporting checklist for ZNE benchmarks.
tldr: This paper identifies a failure mode in Richardson Zero-Noise Extrapolation where noise amplification beyond usable signals leads to artefactual improvements that do not reflect underlying physics.
motivation: Reliable benchmarking of quantum error mitigation requires distinguishing genuine improvements from artefacts of post-processing arithmetic.
method: The authors analyze Richardson ZNE theoretically and experimentally on IQM Euro-Q-Exa hardware, introducing a 'garbage-folding' negative control and a zero-cost check.
result: They show that when noise amplification erodes the signal, ZNE collapses into a fixed rescaling, producing bogus improvements; real hardware measurements confirm overshoots up to 21%.
conclusion: The findings highlight a rarely considered threat to empirical evaluations in quantum computing and provide a reporting checklist for ZNE benchmarks.

title: Quantum Approximate Optimization Via Noise-Directed Adaptive Warm-Starting
authors: Filip B. Maciejewski, Stuart Hadfield, Oscar Wallis, George Pennington, Sebastian Brandhofer, Stefan Woerner, Daniel J. Egger, Davide Venturelli
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Progress towards a quantum advantage using known heuristic methods for combinatorial optimization is impeded by hardware noise and limited qubit count. Here, we propose a noise-aware adaptive approach to quantum approximate optimization, Noise-Directed Adaptive Warm-Starting (ND-AWS), that builds on recent concepts such as Warm-Start QAOA and Noise-Directed Adaptive Remapping. By leveraging bitflip gauge transformations, our algorithm exploits amplitude-damping-like noise components. We experimentally implement high-performance quantum optimization ans\"atze on 100-qubit Ising Hamiltonians, showing that ND-AWS generally improves the performance over a non-gauge-transformed iterative Warm-Starting variant, at no additional circuit cost. This places our results among the highest-quality demonstrations of quantum optimization with similar ans\"atze at this scale. Crucially, the simplicity of the framework opens the door for future enhancements such as adaptive bias schedules, and integration with classical solvers.
tldr: A noise-aware adaptive warm-starting method for QAOA that uses gauge transformations to exploit amplitude-damping noise, demonstrated on 100-qubit Ising Hamiltonians.

method: The algorithm, ND-AWS, applies bitflip gauge transformations to QAOA circuits to turn amplitude-damping noise into a beneficial effect, combined with adaptive warm-starting.
result: ND-AWS improves optimization performance over non-gauge-transformed warm-starting on 100-qubit Ising Hamiltonians at no extra circuit cost.
conclusion: The framework is simple and opens avenues for further enhancements, but the contribution is primarily algorithmic and heuristic rather than a fundamental information-theoretic result.

title: Resource-efficient Simulations Of Particle Scattering On A Digital Quantum Computer
authors: Yahui Chai
Joe Gibbs
Vincent R. Pascuzzi
Zoë Holmes
Stefan Kühn
Francesco Tacchino
Ivano Tavernelli
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 06 July 2026;
tldr: This paper presents resource-efficient quantum algorithms for simulating particle scattering on digital quantum computers.
motivation: Simulating scattering processes is important for high-energy physics but requires large quantum resources; the authors aim to reduce the required qubit count and circuit depth.

title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for semidefinite programming using ADMM and quantum singular value transformation.
motivation: Large-scale SDPs are computationally expensive; quantum computing may offer speedups.
method: Develops an inexact ADMM framework with block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement, using quantum singular value transformation for projection updates.
result: Proves convergence to an optimal solution under strong duality and shows favorable scaling with dimension compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: QADMM is a promising quantum algorithm for large-scale SDPs, but the paper focuses on optimization rather than quantum information theory.
keywords: quantum alternating direction method of multipliers

title: Query And Depth Upper Bounds For Quantum Unitaries Via Grover Search
authors: Gregory Rosenthal
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2144 (2026).

We prove that any [MATH]-qubit unitary can be implemented (i) approximately in time [MATH] with query access to an appropriate classical oracle, and also (ii) exactly by a circuit of depth [MATH] with one- and two-qubit gates and [MATH] ancillae. The proofs involve similar reductions to Grover search. The proof of (ii) also involves a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states using one- and two-qubit gates (in fact, this can be improved to constant depth with the addition of fanout and generalized Toffoli gates) which may be of independent interest. We also prove a matching [MATH] lower bound for (i) and (ii) for a certain class of implementations.

.
tldr: This paper proves upper and lower bounds on query complexity and circuit depth for implementing arbitrary quantum unitaries using Grover search.
motivation: Understanding the resources required to implement arbitrary quantum operations is fundamental to quantum computing and information theory.
method: The authors reduce unitary implementation to Grover search, constructing circuits with linear depth and query access to a classical oracle, and prove matching lower bounds for a class of implementations.

conclusion: The results provide optimal resource bounds for implementing arbitrary unitaries, with implications for quantum circuit synthesis and complexity theory.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A method for temporal coarse-graining of classical stochastic noise in quantum systems, focusing on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with temporally correlated classical noise (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging; this work aims to reduce complexity by integrating out high-frequency noise components.
method: The stochastic noise is expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes; temporal coarse-graining is achieved by conditioning on a coarse realization, separating deterministic and bridge processes, and analytically averaging over bridges.
result: The deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and bridge processes are independent with analytically known correlators, enabling precomputation of noise propagators.
conclusion: The approach provides practical advantages like a simple concatenation rule and is demonstrated with numerical examples, but it is a simulation technique rather than a fundamental information-theoretic result.

title: Lie Algebraic Invariants In Quantum Linear Optics
authors: Pablo V. Parellada, Vicent Gimeno I Garcia, Julio José Moyano-Fernández, And Juan Carlos Garcia-Escartin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2132 (2026).

Quantum linear optics without post-selection is not powerful enough to produce any quantum state from a given input state. This limits its utility since some applications require entangled resources that are difficult to prepare. Thus, a deeper understanding of linear optical state preparation is needed. In this work, we give a recipe to derive conserved quantities in the evolution of arbitrary states along any possible passive linear interferometer. One example of such an invariant is the spectrum of a density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians. These invariants give necessary conditions for exact state preparation: if the input and output states have different invariants, it is impossible to design a passive linear interferometer that evolves one into the other. Moreover, we provide a lower bound to the distance between an output and target state based on the distance between their invariants. This gives a necessary condition for approximate or heralded state preparations. Therefore, the invariants allow us to narrow the search when trying to prepare useful entangled states, like NOON states, from easy-to-prepare states, like Fock states. We conclude that future exact and approximate state preparation methods will need to consider the necessary conditions given by our invariants to weed out impossible linear optical evolutions.

.
tldr: Derives Lie algebraic invariants for passive linear optical networks that constrain state preparation.
motivation: Passive linear optics cannot produce arbitrary quantum states, limiting applications that require entangled resources; understanding the constraints is necessary.
method: Maps the density matrix spectrum onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians and derives conserved quantities under any passive linear interferometer evolution.
result: Provides necessary conditions for exact state preparation and a lower bound on the distance between output and target states based on invariant differences.
conclusion: Future state preparation methods must consider these invariants to rule out impossible evolutions, narrowing the search for useful entangled states like NOON states.

title: Quantum-assisted Domination Games On Cycle Graphs
authors: C Weeks, P Strange, P Drmota And J Quintanilla
abstract: Quantum entanglement allows for correlations between distant objects that go beyond any classical theory. These additional correlations can be exploited to gain practical advantage in certain non-local games. In recent years there has been interest in games defined on graph structures and involving mobile agents. One of these is the graph domination game, where quantum advantage has been discovered recently on some finite graphs by numerical optimisation (Viola and Mironowicz (2024) Phys. Rev. A 109 042201). Here we study quantum advantage in the 1-step, 2-player version of this game, focusing on cycle graphs. We study it numerically, analytically and through the use of noisy, intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) processors. We find explicit strategies and show that they realise the numerical bounds that were found recently for the case of small graphs. We then generalise our strategies to cycles of arbitrary size. Finally, we run our strategies for 5-, 6-, and 7-site cycles on NISQ hardware and find measurable advantage (compared to the optimal classical strategies) in all cases.
tldr: This paper studies quantum advantage in graph domination games on cycle graphs, using numerical, analytical, and NISQ hardware approaches.
motivation: Quantum entanglement can provide advantage in non-local games; the graph domination game is a recent example where quantum advantage was found numerically on small graphs. The authors aim to extend this to cycle graphs of arbitrary size and demonstrate it on NISQ hardware.
method: The authors derive explicit quantum strategies for the 1-step, 2-player domination game on cycle graphs, using numerical optimization, analytical proofs, and implementation on NISQ processors.
result: They find explicit strategies that match numerical bounds for small cycles and generalize to cycles of any size. NISQ experiments on 5-, 6-, and 7-site cycles show measurable quantum advantage over optimal classical strategies.
conclusion: Quantum advantage in graph domination games is robust and scalable to larger cycle graphs, and can be demonstrated on current NISQ devices.

title: Free-fermion Measurement-induced Volume- To Area-law Entanglement Transition In The Presence Of Fermion Interactions

abstract:

In quantum many-body systems, chaotic dynamics that explore all configurations can give way to a localized phase, frozen into a small corner of possibilities. These phases are distinguished by the extensivity of entanglement. Here, the authors argue that the entanglement transition driven by measurements in a broad class of interacting quantum circuits can be described by ree ermions, and they develop a controlled description of the transition via non-Abelian bosonization. The results are also relevant to decodability transitions in certain surface codes with coherent errors.

tldr: This paper studies measurement-induced entanglement transitions in interacting fermion systems, mapping them to free-fermion transitions via non-Abelian bosonization.
motivation: Understanding measurement-induced phase transitions in quantum many-body systems is a key topic in quantum thermodynamics and information processing, but the paper focuses on entanglement dynamics in interacting circuits.
method: The authors use non-Abelian bosonization to map the interacting fermion problem to a free-fermion one, enabling a controlled description of the entanglement transition.
result: They show that the measurement-induced volume-to-area law entanglement transition in a class of interacting quantum circuits can be described by free fermions, and relate it to decodability transitions in surface codes.
conclusion: The work provides a tractable model for measurement-induced transitions in interacting systems, but its primary contribution is to many-body physics rather than to information thermodynamics or quantum information theory directly.

title: Machine Learning Decoding Of Circuit-Level Noise For Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: John Blue, Harshil Avlani, Zhiyang He, Liu Ziyin, And Isaac L. Chuang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2149 (2026).

Fault-tolerant quantum computers will depend crucially on the performance of the classical decoding algorithm which takes in the results of measurements and outputs corrections to the errors inferred to have occurred. Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: This paper applies machine learning decoding to bivariate bicycle codes, a type of quantum LDPC code, achieving lower logical error rates and faster runtime than BP-OSD on small codes.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient decoders for quantum error correction codes; machine learning decoders have shown promise for surface codes but not yet for QLDPC codes.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is trained to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes, using syndrome data to predict error corrections.
result: On the [[144,12,12]] BB code, the ML decoder achieves logical error rates almost 10 times lower than BP-OSD and is an order of magnitude faster, though performance degrades on larger codes.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures or training procedures.

Compared to a magic cat state stabiliser decomposition of all [MATH] non-Clifford spiders ([MATH] terms required), this is more than [MATH] times reduction in the number of terms. Our stabiliser decomposition has the advantage of representing the final non-Clifford state (in light of circuit errors) as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams. This will be useful in simulating the escape stage of magic state cultivation, where one needs to port the resultant state of cultivation into a larger Clifford circuit with many more qubits. Still, it's necessary to only track [MATH] Clifford terms. Our result sheds light on the simulability of operationally relevant, high [MATH]-count quantum circuits with some internal structure. Finally, we provide numerical results for full non-Clifford stabiliser rank simulation based on [MATH] along with optimisations using our cutting decompositions. Nearly [MATH] shots per second can be obtained on a laptop for the smaller [MATH] circuits at uniform circuit level noise [MATH], making it only [MATH][MATH] times slower than its (circuit-unspecific and un-optimised) fully Clifford proxy simulation via [MATH] using [MATH] gates.

tldr: This paper presents methods to simulate magic state cultivation circuits using a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, achieving a significant reduction in the number of terms compared to full stabiliser decomposition.
motivation: Magic state cultivation is a key technique for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating these circuits is computationally expensive due to the high non-Clifford gate count. The authors aim to reduce simulation cost by exploiting structure in the circuits.
method: The authors develop stabiliser decompositions that represent the non-Clifford state as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, using cutting techniques to reduce the number of terms. They also provide numerical simulations with optimisations.
result: They achieve a reduction in the number of terms by more than a factor of 1000 compared to naive decomposition, and can simulate nearly 1000 shots per second on a laptop for small circuits at uniform noise.

title: Cosma: Communication-aware Optimization Of Fermionic Simulation Kernels For Modular Quantum Architectures

In such systems, inter-core quantum communication becomes a major performance bottleneck. In this work, we present COSMA, a communication-aware compilation framework for fermionic simulation kernels targeting modular quantum architectures. Our approach jointly optimizes fermion-to-qubit mapping, Pauli scheduling, and qubit allocation to minimize inter-core state transfers. Evaluated on molecular benchmarks, COSMA achieves up to [MATH] reduction in communication cost compared to state-of-the-art baselines, with a median improvement of [MATH]. title: Green’s Function Methods For Computing Supercurrents In Josephson Junctions
authors: Eduardo R Mucciolo, Jouko Nieminen, Xiao Xiao, Wei-Chi Chiu, Michael N Leuenberger And Arun Bansil
abstract: Interest in Josephson junctions (JJs) has increased rapidly in recent years not only because of their use in qubits and other quantum devices but also due to the unique physics supported by the JJs. The advent of various novel quantum materials for both the barrier region and the superconducting leads has led to the possibility of adding new functionalities to the JJs. Thus, there is a growing need for accurate modeling of the JJs and related systems to enable their predictive control and atomistic level understanding. This review presents an in-depth discussion of a Green’s-function-based formalism for computing supercurrents in JJs. The formulation is tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations and encompasses both dc and ac supercurrents. We hope that this review will provide a timely and comprehensive reference for researchers as well as beginning practitioners interested in Green’s-function-based methods to model supercurrents in JJs.
tldr: A review of Green's function methods for computing supercurrents in Josephson junctions, focusing on large-scale atomistic simulations.
motivation: Josephson junctions are key components in qubits and quantum devices, and accurate modeling is needed for predictive control and understanding of novel quantum materials.
method: The paper presents a Green's-function-based formalism tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations to compute both dc and ac supercurrents in Josephson junctions.
result: The formalism enables accurate modeling of supercurrents in Josephson junctions with various barrier and lead materials.
conclusion: The review provides a comprehensive reference for researchers interested in Green's-function-based methods for modeling supercurrents in Josephson junctions.

title: Finite-time Cooling And Accessibility Of The Stripe Phase In The Ising Antiferromagnet

abstract: ArXiv:2607.09411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The finite-rate cooling dynamics of the triangular-lattice [MATH] Ising antiferromagnet is studied under local Metropolis updates. Although an antiferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor coupling selects a stripe phase in equilibrium, the simulations show that this phase is not automatically reached on finite time scales. A kinetic stripe-formation time [MATH] is defined from the probability of obtaining a globally stripe-ordered final state. This time shifts to much slower cooling as the system size increases and to faster cooling as [MATH] increases. The size dependence is compatible with a coarsening-controlled process, with an effective growth at least quadratic in L over the simulated range. Real-space morphology and fixed-temperature diagnostics show that failed trajectories are not simply disordered states: they often contain locally stripe-ordered domains separated by residual walls or competing orientations. In the weak-[MATH] regime, the system can restore the local nearest-neighbor frustrated constraint while still failing to select a global stripe sector. These results separate three processes that are usually conflated: energetic degeneracy lifting by [MATH], local constraint restoration, and global stripe-orientation selection under local dynamics.
tldr: This paper studies finite-time cooling dynamics of the triangular-lattice Ising antiferromagnet, focusing on the accessibility of the stripe phase under local Metropolis updates.
motivation: Understanding how ordered phases emerge under finite-rate cooling is important for non-equilibrium thermodynamics, but the paper's focus on a specific classical spin model and coarsening dynamics is not directly aligned with the researcher's core interests in quantum information thermodynamics.
method: Monte Carlo simulations of the triangular-lattice Ising model with antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor couplings, using local Metropolis updates to study cooling at finite rates.
result: The stripe phase is not automatically reached on finite time scales; a kinetic stripe-formation time is defined, which scales with system size and coupling strength, and failed trajectories contain locally ordered domains.
conclusion: Three processes (energetic degeneracy lifting, local constraint restoration, and global stripe selection) are separated, showing that local dynamics can fail to select the global stripe phase even when local constraints are satisfied.

title: Low-frequency Electric Field Sensing With A Rydberg Beam
authors: Jeremy Glick, John R. Dickson, Josie Wood, And Paul Kunz
abstract:
Author(s): Jeremy Glick, John R. Dickson, Josie Wood, and Paul Kunz

The authors perform low-frequency electric field sensing using ionization detection on a collimated beam of Rydberg atoms. This reduces challenges associated with electric field screening effects present in warm vapor cells containing alkali-metal atoms.


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012608] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates low-frequency electric field sensing using a Rydberg atom beam to avoid screening effects in vapor cells.
motivation: Low-frequency electric field sensing is important for various applications, but traditional Rydberg atom vapor cells suffer from electric field screening due to dielectric windows and metal walls.
method: The authors use a collimated beam of Rydberg atoms and detect ionization to measure electric fields, which reduces screening effects present in warm vapor cells.
result: The Rydberg beam method successfully measures low-frequency electric fields with reduced screening, improving sensitivity and accuracy.
conclusion: The Rydberg beam approach offers a practical solution for low-frequency electric field sensing, overcoming limitations of vapor cell techniques.

title: Multiple Majorana Zero Modes Induced By Geometric Spin-orbit Coupling In Helical Nanoribbon-superconductor Hybrids
authors: Kai-Yuan Zhang, Shu-Zheng Zhou, Xi Sun, And Hua-Hua Fu
abstract:
Author(s): Kai-Yuan Zhang, Shu-Zheng Zhou, Xi Sun, and Hua-Hua Fu

Majorana zero modes (MZMs), which serve as a key platform for realizing fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, remain challenging in excitation and regulation. In this work, we propose chiral nanoribbon-superconductor hybrids as a platform for realizing multiple MZMs. The hybrid system compri…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 065408] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a chiral nanoribbon-superconductor hybrid platform to realize multiple Majorana zero modes via geometric spin-orbit coupling.
motivation: Majorana zero modes are promising for topological quantum computing but remain difficult to excite and control. The authors aim to design a new platform that can host multiple MZMs.
method: The hybrid system consists of a helical nanoribbon with geometric spin-orbit coupling placed on a superconductor. The authors theoretically analyze the band structure and topological phases to identify conditions for MZM emergence.
result: Multiple Majorana zero modes are predicted to appear at the ends of the nanoribbon, tunable by the spin-orbit coupling strength and chemical potential.
conclusion: The proposed platform offers a controllable way to generate multiple MZMs, potentially advancing topological quantum computing hardware.

title: Toric Code Under Antiferromagnetic Isotropic Heisenberg Interactions
authors: Won Jang, Robert Peters, And Thore Posske
abstract:
Author(s): Won Jang, Robert Peters, and Thore Posske

We investigate the impact of an isotropic antiferromagnetic Heisenberg perturbation on the toric code, focusing on the resulting quantum phase transition and the nature of the phase that emerges beyond topological order. Using neural-network quantum states, we compute ground states over a wide range…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033008] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the effect of an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg perturbation on the toric code, revealing a quantum phase transition to a trivial paramagnet.
motivation: To understand how perturbations affect topological order in the toric code and characterize the resulting phase.
method: Uses neural-network quantum states to compute ground states and analyze phase transitions via order parameters and entanglement entropy.
result: Finds a first-order quantum phase transition from the topological phase to a trivial paramagnet, with no intermediate phase.
conclusion: The isotropic Heisenberg perturbation destroys topological order directly, without passing through any other nontrivial phase.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and optical control.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated materials, which may reveal novel phases and functionalities.
method: Comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances, discussing nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways using static or periodic fields.
result: Key mechanisms governing photodoped carrier evolution and emergence of metastable states with superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders are identified.
conclusion: Photoexcitation provides a powerful tool to manipulate Mott insulators, but the work is primarily a materials physics review without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics of information processing.

title: The Quantum Harmonic Oscillator In A Dissipative Bath Of Anyon Pairs
authors: A Pelster And M Thorwart N-H Meyer
abstract: We generalize the formalism of open quantum systems to introduce anyon baths. In particular, we work out a dissipative anyon bath composed of independent pairs of one-dimensional Grundberg–Hansson harmonically bound anyons, which are characterized by one statistical parameter. Using a mapping of these anyons to a bosonic bath with rescaled oscillator frequencies, we show that the original bilinear system-bath coupling assumes a particular non-polynomial form. To determine the relaxation properties, we use the imaginary-time path integral formalism together with a generalization of Wick’s theorem in the form of a smearing formula. The latter allows to approximately calculate the anyon bath spectral density, which acquires a nontrivial temperature dependence. The corresponding relaxation dynamics of the dissipative harmonic oscillator in an anyon bath is found. Well defined limits are revealed for both low and high temperatures. Anyonic features turn out to be most pronounced in the regime of intermediate temperatures.
tldr: This paper studies a quantum harmonic oscillator coupled to a dissipative bath of anyon pairs, deriving the spectral density and relaxation dynamics.
motivation: To extend open quantum system formalism to anyon baths, which are exotic quasiparticles with fractional statistics, and understand their effect on relaxation.
method: Uses a mapping of anyon pairs to a bosonic bath with rescaled frequencies, then applies imaginary-time path integrals and a generalized Wick's theorem to compute the spectral density.
result: The anyon bath spectral density acquires a nontrivial temperature dependence, and the relaxation dynamics of the oscillator is found, with anyonic features most pronounced at intermediate temperatures.
conclusion: The work generalizes dissipative quantum systems to anyon baths, but the connection to information thermodynamics is weak; it is more a study of open quantum systems with exotic statistics.

title: A Novel Parallel Qcnn Architecture With Efficient Classical Simulability
authors: Hiu Yung Wong Lawrence Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a study of an implementation of a novel Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) for binary classification of images from the Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology (MNIST) dataset. Using a novel architecture inspired by previous QCNN and classical convolutional neural network (CNN) implementations, we use a hierarchical partitioning approach to implement a QCNN circuit that can be approximated and simulated efficiently on a classical machine for a large problem. First, the original image is partitioned such that each process handles a smaller portion of the image, which is encoded into independent states. Then, these partitions merge and combine, resulting in states that contain information from both partitions while halving the number of processes. After repeating this until one process remains, we reduce the dimensionality of the state until a single qubit remains for measurement. Using this approach, we can use multiple processes in parallel to simulate a large QCNN program without the need for exponentially growing hardware requirements as the number of qubits increases. In our work, we use this scheme to train a 128-qubit model, which is impossible to run on any classical supercomputer without the novel architecture. We also explore the impact of this new model architecture on prediction accuracy by training it to perform binary classification on the MNIST dataset with a small number of qubits, and comparing it to a model without partitioning. Our initial findings show that partitioning images into smaller sub-images with this architecture does not degrade the model's performance and sometimes even improves it, likely because it reduces the Barren plateaus issue in the partitioning process.
tldr: A parallel QCNN architecture for MNIST classification that uses hierarchical partitioning to enable classical simulation of up to 128 qubits.
motivation: To overcome the exponential resource requirements of simulating large QCNNs on classical computers and to explore whether partitioning affects accuracy.
method: The image is partitioned into sub-images, each encoded into independent quantum states; these are merged hierarchically, reducing the number of processes until a single qubit remains for measurement.
result: The 128-qubit model can be simulated classically using the novel architecture, and partitioning does not degrade accuracy; it sometimes improves it, possibly by mitigating barren plateaus.
conclusion: The proposed parallel QCNN architecture enables efficient classical simulation of large QCNNs without accuracy loss, offering a practical approach for image classification.

title: Quantum Logic As The Logic Of Contexts
authors: Haruki Emori, Atsushi Iriki, Andrei Khrennikov, Kazunori Kondo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum logic is usually presented as a non-classical departure from ordinary reasoning forced on us by quantum mechanics, with classical logic kept as the secure starting point. We argue for the opposite order of explanation in a finite and fully computable setting. The free orthomodular lattice on two generators has ninety-six elements, the direct product of a six-element non-distributive factor and a sixteen-element Boolean factor. Reading the first factor as a register of contexts and the second as Boolean content, we obtain a calculus whose elements are context--bit-vector pairs and whose operations act component by component. With this calculus we establish three results. First, we classify the six layers by commutativity, identifying the central kernel of context-neutral propositions together with a dual central layer in which all complementary contexts are present. Second, we show that orthocomplementation rearranges the layers exactly as the complementation of the small factor rearranges its elements, which makes the duality among the layers rigid rather than accidental. Third, we prove that the operation forgetting the context is a surjective homomorphism of orthocomplemented lattices whose quotient is the classical Boolean algebra, so that classical logic is a six-to-one, information-losing image of the contextual calculus.
tldr: The paper presents a finite, computable quantum logic based on the free orthomodular lattice on two generators, interpreting it as a calculus of contexts and Boolean content.
motivation: To challenge the conventional view that quantum logic is a non-classical departure from classical logic, instead arguing that classical logic is a coarse-grained image of a more fundamental contextual logic.
method: The authors analyze the structure of the free orthomodular lattice on two generators, decompose it into a product of a six-element non-distributive factor and a sixteen-element Boolean factor, and define operations componentwise.
result: They classify the six layers by commutativity, show that orthocomplementation rearranges layers rigidly, and prove that forgetting the context yields a surjective homomorphism onto classical Boolean algebra.
conclusion: Classical logic emerges as a six-to-one information-losing quotient of a contextual quantum logic, reversing the usual explanatory order.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Synthetic Data Generation Using Quantum Circuit Born Machines For Imbalanced Tabular Learning
authors: Tanapol Nuatho, Narisorn Sangnakara, Prapong Prechaprapranwong, Rajchawit Sarochawikasit
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data scarcity and class imbalance are persistent challenges in machine learning that degrade model generalization and introduce predictive bias. We present a hybrid quantum-classical framework for synthetic data generation using a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) to address these limitations. The proposed approach exploits quantum mechanical properties -- superposition and entanglement -- within a parameterized variational quantum circuit to model complex probability distributions that are difficult for classical generative methods to capture. Experiments are conducted on two tabular benchmark datasets: the Iris dataset and the Telco Customer Churn dataset. Preprocessing includes normalization and PCA-based dimensionality reduction to enable efficient basis encoding for quantum circuits. The QCBM is trained by minimizing Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between real and generated data distributions using a gradient-based parameter-shift optimization rule. Augmenting training data with QCBM-generated synthetic samples at 40-50% of the minority class improves F1-score by approximately 5-15% and minority-class recall by 10-25%. Cross-domain evaluations (Train on Synthetic, Test on Real; and Train on Real, Test on Synthetic) reveal a performance gap of only 3-10%, indicating strong distributional fidelity. Comparative analysis against classical oversampling methods -- SMOTE, Borderline-SMOTE, KMeansSMOTE, and SVM-SMOTE -- shows that QCBM achieves competitive classification performance and produces lower Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) on the Telco dataset, suggesting superior structural similarity in certain imbalanced settings. These findings establish QCBM as a viable complementary tool for data augmentation, particularly for low-dimensional structured tabular data with class imbalance.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical framework using Quantum Circuit Born Machines for synthetic data generation to address class imbalance in tabular datasets.
motivation: Data scarcity and class imbalance degrade machine learning model performance; existing classical oversampling methods have limitations.
method: A parameterized variational quantum circuit (QCBM) is trained by minimizing KL divergence between real and generated distributions using gradient-based parameter-shift rules, with PCA-based dimensionality reduction for basis encoding.
result: QCBM-generated synthetic samples improve F1-score by 5-15% and minority-class recall by 10-25% on Iris and Telco datasets, with competitive performance compared to SMOTE variants and lower MMD on Telco.
conclusion: QCBM is a viable complementary tool for data augmentation in low-dimensional tabular data with class imbalance, but the contribution is incremental and not deeply tied to core quantum information theory.

title: Universal Neural Network Based Calibration And Control Of Programmable Classical And Quantum Photonic Integrated Processors
authors: Jos\'e Roberto Rausell-Campo, Daniele Melati, Bhavin Shastri, Daniel P\'erez-L\'opez, Jos\'e Capmany Francoy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient calibration and control of programmable photonic integrated circuits are fundamental for scaling quantum and classical optical computing processors. While neural network-based models offer an architecture-agnostic solution, existing approaches suffer from limited learning and generalization capabilities due to the many-to-one mapping problem between sets of control signals and optical responses, and biased training datasets derived from uniform current sampling. In this work, we propose a universal calibration and control framework employing tandem neural networks combined with two novel data generation strategies: architecture-aware sampling based on Haar measure principles, and optimized sampling, a physics-agnostic approach utilizing differential evolution. We experimentally validate these methods on 3x3 and 4x4 coherent MZI meshes, demonstrating that our approach addresses the sampling bias inherent in previous works. When evaluated using random unitary matrices, our solution outperforms standard uniform sampling baselines by ~2 bits of precision. Furthermore, we experimentally extend the application of this framework to coherent detection, achieving precise control over both amplitude and phase, and validate its impact on photonic neural network tasks.
tldr: A neural network framework for calibrating and controlling programmable photonic integrated circuits, validated on MZI meshes.
motivation: Efficient calibration and control of programmable photonic circuits are needed for scaling quantum and classical optical computing, but existing neural network approaches suffer from limited generalization due to biased training data.
method: The authors propose a tandem neural network with two novel data generation strategies: architecture-aware sampling based on Haar measure principles and physics-agnostic optimized sampling using differential evolution.
result: Experimental validation on 3x3 and 4x4 MZI meshes shows ~2 bits precision improvement over standard uniform sampling, and the framework is extended to coherent detection for photonic neural network tasks.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a universal, architecture-agnostic solution for calibration and control of programmable photonic circuits, with potential applications in quantum and classical optical computing.

title: Qma Lower Bounds For Batch Verification Via Approximate Degree
authors: Mark Bun, Mandar Juvekar, Samuel King
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study batch verification in QMA query and communication complexity, where the goal is to understand how the resources needed to verify [MATH] copies of a Boolean function [MATH] depend on [MATH]. We give a general technique for proving lower bounds on the witness-query tradeoff needed to batch verify a function [MATH] in terms of its approximate degree. Applying this technique to an explicit family of DNF formulas [MATH], we show that attempting to save even a constant factor on the witness length of the baseline approach to batch verifying [MATH] necessitates a large polynomial increase in the query cost. We also obtain new lower bounds on the QMA query complexity of read-once CNF formulas and on the surjectivity and [MATH]-element distinctness functions. Our lower bounds also lift to give communication analogs of these results.
tldr: This paper studies QMA lower bounds for batch verification using approximate degree, focusing on query and communication complexity.
motivation: To understand the resource trade-offs in verifying multiple copies of a Boolean function in the QMA model.
method: Develops a general technique for proving lower bounds on witness-query tradeoffs based on approximate degree, applied to DNF formulas and other functions.
result: Shows that saving a constant factor in witness length for batch verification of certain DNF formulas requires a large polynomial increase in query cost; also obtains new lower bounds for read-once CNF, surjectivity, and k-element distinctness.
conclusion: The results provide fundamental limits on batch verification in QMA, highlighting the difficulty of reducing witness size without increasing query complexity.

title: Bose–Einstein Condensate Of Ultracold Sodium–rubidium Molecules With Tunable Dipolar Interactions
authors: Zhaopeng Shi
