title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism, which has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena.
method: The paper is a review that surveys experimental and theoretical progress in 2D van der Waals magnets, including topics like topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, and spintronics.
result: The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.
conclusion: 2D van der Waals magnets are a rich platform for studying magnetism in reduced dimensions, with potential for future technologies.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This review paper presents a unified perspective on radiation forces and torques in optical and acoustic wave fields, focusing on particle manipulation.
motivation: Understanding how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in wave fields induce forces and torques on particles is fundamental for applications like optical trapping and acoustic sorting.
method: The authors review theoretical frameworks and experimental demonstrations of radiation forces and torques, drawing parallels between optics and acoustics.
result: The paper provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms behind radiation-induced forces and torques, including pulling forces and spin-induced torques.
conclusion: The unified perspective highlights common principles across optics and acoustics, offering insights for future applications in particle manipulation.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A review of exactly solvable quantum many-body dynamics using space-time duality and brickwork quantum circuits.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; this review aims to provide a unified pedagogical view based on space-time duality.
method: The review discusses discretizing time evolution in lattice systems, treating space and time on the same footing, and focuses on brickwork quantum circuits as a framework.
result: The paper presents a pedagogical overview of how space-time duality enables exact solutions for certain interacting many-body systems.
conclusion: Space-time duality and brickwork circuits offer a powerful analogy with quantum computation for understanding quantum many-body dynamics.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on their exotic electronic states and many-body phenomena.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual states in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and orbital antiferromagnetism.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, analyzing electronic band structures, correlation effects, and topological properties.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic phenomena including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, and amplified Hall effects.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for studying strongly correlated and topological physics, but the paper is primarily a materials science review without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems in chemistry, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: To unify diverse approaches for modeling complex systems with many interacting agents under a single field-theoretic framework.
method: The authors review and apply field-theoretic methods, such as path integrals and Doi-Peliti formalism, to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems.
result: The review demonstrates how field theories can handle chemical systems and have applications in ecology and epidemiology.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods provide a powerful unified framework for studying stochastic reaction-diffusion systems across various disciplines.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the Universe, and their properties provide information about matter under extreme compression.
method: The review summarizes constraints from gravitational-wave signals of binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, comparing them to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: The measurements constrain masses, radii, and central densities of neutron stars, which are compared to theoretical predictions.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine our understanding of the dense matter equation of state.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation.
motivation: To provide an updated overview of spin-glass research and highlight the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation.
method: Review of experimental, theoretical, and large-scale simulation studies in spin glasses.
result: Summarizes progress in understanding spin-glass dynamics and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich field with broad applications, and continued interdisciplinary collaboration is essential.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are a type of quantum spin liquid with potential applications in topological quantum computing.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental realizations in materials, highlighting chiral edge modes and other topological features.
result: The review summarizes key candidate materials and their properties, emphasizing the broad topological phenomena observed.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids are a rich field with many open questions, and the review serves as a guide for future research.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, with applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key nonradiative process in photophysics, and understanding its theoretical underpinnings is important for applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models describing internal conversion, covering different facets of the nonradiative mechanism.
result: The review provides an overview of current theoretical approaches and an outlook on their incorporation into application-oriented studies.
conclusion: Theoretical methods for internal conversion are mature but need to be better integrated into applied research in photonics and energy harvesting.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum properties and functionalities of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their topological nature and potential applications.
motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for spintronic devices, but their quantum aspects are less explored; this review aims to bridge that gap.
method: The paper surveys theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion formation, quantum interactions, and quantum features of skyrmions themselves.
result: It highlights quantum effects such as tunneling, superposition, and entanglement in skyrmion systems, and discusses their potential for quantum information processing.
conclusion: Magnetic skyrmions exhibit rich quantum behavior that could be harnessed for future quantum technologies, but the field is still nascent.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, including their possible mediation by exotic bosons and implications for dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy, and to probe discrete fundamental symmetries, by searching for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model.
method: The paper reviews a wide range of theoretical models and experimental techniques used to search for spin-dependent exotic interactions, including precision measurements with atomic, molecular, and optical systems.
result: The review summarizes current constraints on various exotic boson-mediated interactions and outlines future experimental directions.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain an active area of research with potential to reveal new physics beyond the standard model, but no definitive evidence has been found yet.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations by examining underlying assumptions.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but many measurements exceed them; understanding why can lead to new materials with enhanced properties.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of circumstances where measured properties exceed classical bounds and identifies which assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linear response) are violated in each case.
result: It shows that apparent violations arise because measurements are made in ways that violate the assumptions behind the bounds, and that materials can be designed to exploit these violations.
conclusion: The findings clarify the limits of classical thermodynamic bounds and provide a framework for developing materials with properties beyond conventional limits.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical implementations of fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems for simulating quantum many-body physics.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body phenomena in nonstandard geometries that are difficult to realize in conventional settings, such as topology and gravity analogs.
method: The paper surveys various platforms (cold atoms, photonics, electronic systems) and techniques for engineering synthetic lattices with fractal, curved, or higher-dimensional geometries.
result: It highlights recent progress in simulating exotic geometries and discusses open challenges and future directions.
conclusion: Synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries offers a powerful tool for studying fundamental physics, but many experimental and theoretical challenges remain.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical and experimental efforts to study gravity's effects on massive quantum systems, focusing on tests of quantum gravity.
motivation: Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force, and massive quantum systems may serve as probes to study gravity's quantum nature.
method: The paper reviews theories of gravity-induced decoherence, collapse models, and entanglement mediation, along with experimental platforms such as matter-wave interferometry and optomechanics.
result: It summarizes the current state of experiments testing whether gravity causes decoherence or mediates entanglement, and outlines future directions.
conclusion: Experiments with massive quantum systems can guide the theoretical description of gravity on a laboratory scale, but no definitive results are yet available.

title: On The Significance Of Wigner’s Friend In Contexts Beyond Quantum Foundations
authors: Caroline L. Jones And Markus P. Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2147 (2026).

There has been a surge of recent interest in the Wigner's Friend paradox, sparking several novel thought experiments and no-go theorems. The main narrative has been that Wigner's Friend highlights a counterintuitive feature that is unique to quantum theory, and which is closely related to the quantum measurement problem. Here, we challenge this view. We argue that the gist of the Wigner's Friend paradox can be reproduced without assuming quantum physics, and that it underlies a much broader class of enigmas in the foundations of physics and philosophy. To show this, we first consider several recently proposed Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios, and demonstrate that some of their implications for the absoluteness of observations can be reproduced by classical thought experiments that involve the duplication of agents. Crucially, some of these classical scenarios are technologically much easier to implement than their quantum counterparts. Then, we argue that the essential structural ingredient of all these scenarios is a feature that we call "Restriction A": that a physical theory cannot give us a probabilistic description of the observations of all agents. Finally, we argue that this difficulty is at the core of other puzzles in the foundations of physics and philosophy, and demonstrate this explicitly for cosmology's Boltzmann brain problem. Our analysis suggests that Wigner's Friend should be studied in a larger context, addressing a frontier of human knowledge beyond quantum foundations: to obtain reliable predictions for experiments in which these predictions can be privately but not intersubjectively verified.

.
tldr: The paper argues that the Wigner's Friend paradox is not unique to quantum theory and can be reproduced classically, suggesting broader implications for foundations of physics and philosophy.
motivation: To challenge the view that Wigner's Friend highlights a uniquely quantum feature and to show its relevance to other puzzles like the Boltzmann brain problem.
method: The authors analyze Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios and construct classical thought experiments with agent duplication, identifying a structural feature called 'Restriction A'.
result: They demonstrate that some implications of Wigner's Friend can be reproduced classically, and that 'Restriction A' underlies other foundational puzzles.
conclusion: Wigner's Friend should be studied in a broader context beyond quantum foundations, addressing issues of private versus intersubjective verification.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: This paper presents PyOpticL, an open-source Python library for modular optical layout, and demonstrates its use for building a laser system for trapped-ion qubit operations.
motivation: Complex optical design in quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and scalability.
method: The authors developed PyOpticL, a code-to-CAD optical layout tool that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing, and created modular drop-in optical baseplates for common subsystems. They demonstrated the system with a strontium trapped-ion setup.
result: The modular optical system achieved over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates and was used for laser cooling and qubit state detection.
conclusion: PyOpticL enables a new paradigm of design abstraction for engineering optical systems, fostering open-source collaborative hardware design for quantum computing and AMO physics.

title: Sorting Prolate And Oblate Spheroids With A Diatomic Gas In A Magnetic Field
authors: Ruben Lier
abstract: For a gas of diatomic particles with a nonzero magnetic moment, the Senftleben–Beenakker effect implies that transport can be affected by a magnetic field even when the particles are charge neutral. In such a gas, two independent anisotropic odd viscosities are allowed by symmetry and can have opposite signs. We study the resulting odd-viscous Stokes flow around spheroids in the regime where the odd viscosities are small compared to the shear viscosity. Using a perturbative expansion around the spherical solution and the Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we compute the lift forces on oblate and prolate spheroids for general values of the two odd viscosity coefficients. We show that the resulting Hall angles can differ for oblate and prolate spheroids, implying that sedimentation in a diatomic gas subject to a background magnetic field can separate particles according to shape.
tldr: This paper studies odd-viscous Stokes flow around spheroids in a diatomic gas under a magnetic field, showing shape-based separation via Hall angles.
motivation: To understand how odd viscosities in a neutral diatomic gas affect transport and enable particle separation by shape.
method: Perturbative expansion around spherical solution and Lorentz reciprocal theorem to compute lift forces on spheroids for general odd viscosity coefficients.
result: Hall angles differ for oblate and prolate spheroids, implying shape-based separation during sedimentation in a magnetic field.
conclusion: The Senftleben–Beenakker effect can be exploited to separate particles by shape using a magnetic field.

title: Readjustment Of Intrinsic Activity Parameters Governs The Rectified Transport In Asymmetric Ratchets
authors: Yunyan Chen, Xiaoyuan Yu, Fengguo Li And Baoquan Ai
abstract: The rectified transport of active Brownian particles (ABPs) in asymmetric ratchets has been extensively studied. However, most existing literature regulates rectification by designing different structural boundaries. In this work, we shift the research perspective to the internal properties of ABPs and explore the influence of their internal physical parameters on the transport process. Using the vibration-driven vehicle (VDV) as a macroscopic experimental model for ABPs, we systematically adjust the overall mass and position of center of mass of the VDV to reveal its underlying dynamic mechanism. Through long-time dynamic tracking, we identify a ‘parameters readjustment effect’: an increase in mass weakens the particle’s average velocity and persistence length, ultimately driving the active system into a noise-dominated macroscopic localized state. More importantly, the shift of the center of mass induces persistent translational–rotational coupling in the VDV, leading to an anomalous non-monotonic reentrant phase transition in the rectification probability of the system. Our study reveals that this anomalous transport law is fundamentally governed by the dynamic spatial competition between the intrinsic chiral orbit radius of the VDV and the geometric characteristic scale of the channel. Coarse-grained ABP numerical simulations reproduce the overall experimental trends. This work indicates that load-induced parameters evolution is not merely a physical perturbation, but a core dimension that determines macroscopic transport behavior, providing physical insights and principles for going beyond purely geometric design constraints and designing efficient active rectification systems.
tldr: This paper studies rectified transport of active Brownian particles in asymmetric ratchets by adjusting internal parameters like mass and center of mass, revealing a 'parameters readjustment effect' and anomalous reentrant phase transitions.
motivation: Most existing work on active ratchets focuses on structural boundaries; this work shifts to internal properties of active particles to understand their influence on transport.
method: Using a vibration-driven vehicle as a macroscopic experimental model for active Brownian particles, the authors systematically vary mass and center of mass position, and perform coarse-grained numerical simulations.
result: Increasing mass weakens average velocity and persistence length, leading to a noise-dominated localized state; shifting center of mass induces translational-rotational coupling causing non-monotonic reentrant phase transitions in rectification probability.
conclusion: Internal parameter evolution is a core determinant of macroscopic transport behavior, offering principles for designing efficient active rectification systems beyond geometric constraints.

title: Unlocking Complex Optical Vortices With Flat Optics
authors: Hammad Ahmed, Shumei Chen, Xibin Yang And Xianzhong Chen
abstract: Optical vortices (OVs) possess spiral wavefronts and quantized orbital angular momentum (OAM), allowing them to act as key carriers of information and enabling light to possess high-dimensional degrees of freedom. In the past decade, there has been a growing interest in investigating complex OVs. Nevertheless, conventional methods for generating such beams are limited by bulky setups, high costs, and restricted control. Optical metasurfaces have emerged as promising candidates to overcome these challenges in a compact and cost-effective platform with enhanced control. This review begins by presenting an advanced platform designed for manipulating OVs and then discusses emerging types of OVs, including composite, grafted, and comb-like structured light beams, as well as multispectral and arbitrarily shaped OVs, along with nonlinear metasurface approaches. Next, we review the recent progress in OAM detection and mode discrimination, highlighting current challenges for high-capacity OAM systems. After that, we emphasize key applications ranging from OAM-based holography for optical encryption to super-resolution microscopy, structured-light trapping, and quantum state engineering. Finally, we critically identify the key challenges and future prospects for metasurface-enabled OV technologies.
tldr: A review of metasurface-based generation and detection of complex optical vortices for high-dimensional information encoding.
motivation: Conventional methods for generating complex optical vortices are bulky and costly; metasurfaces offer a compact, cost-effective platform with enhanced control.
method: The paper reviews recent progress in metasurface designs for generating composite, grafted, comb-like, multispectral, and arbitrarily shaped optical vortices, as well as OAM detection and mode discrimination techniques.
result: Metasurface-enabled OV technologies enable applications in OAM-based holography, super-resolution microscopy, structured-light trapping, and quantum state engineering.
conclusion: Metasurface platforms hold promise for advancing OV-based information technologies, but challenges remain in scalability and integration.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on their stability and intensity distributions.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which have not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically find families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons.
result: Two classes of stable vortex solitons are found, with stability intervals broadening as discrete rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory to quasicrystals with topological deformations, offering potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Charting Light Harvesting In Purple Bacteria In Vivo
authors: Romain Rouxeljulian Lüttigmichael R. Jonesdonatas Zigmantasahttps://ror.org/012a77v79division Of Chemical Physics, Department Of Chemistry, Lund University, Lund Se-221 00, Swedenbhttps://ror.org/03c4mmv16department Of Physics, University Of Ottawa, Ottawa, ON K1N 6N5, Canadachttps://ror.org/0524sp257school Of Biochemistry, Biomedical Sciences Building, University Of Bristol, Bristol BS8 1TD, United Kingdom
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 27, July 2026.
SignificanceTwo-dimensional electronic spectroscopy emerged as the method of choice to unravel molecular couplings and energy transfer pathways in photosynthetic systems. Experiments on individual photosynthetic complexes have been very successful, but ...
tldr: This paper uses two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy to study light harvesting in purple bacteria in vivo.
motivation: Understanding energy transfer in photosynthetic systems is important for biology and potentially for artificial photosynthesis.
method: Two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy experiments on intact purple bacteria.
result: The study maps energy transfer pathways and molecular couplings in vivo.
conclusion: The work provides insights into natural light harvesting but does not directly address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Brownian Bridge For Coherent State Path Integral Monte Carlo
authors: Riccardo Fantoni
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a new Brownian bridge construction for our newly devised Coherent States Path Integral Monte Carlo algorithm. We apply it to the numerically exact calculation of the thermodynamic properties of the Helium fluid on a plane at low non zero temperature. We find very good agreement with the conventional plane waves path integral Monte Carlo results.
tags: coherent state path integral Monte Carlo
tldr: This paper proposes a Brownian bridge construction for coherent state path integral Monte Carlo to compute thermodynamic properties of helium fluid.
motivation: To improve the efficiency and accuracy of path integral Monte Carlo simulations for quantum fluids using coherent states.
method: A new Brownian bridge algorithm is developed within the coherent state path integral Monte Carlo framework.
result: The method yields very good agreement with conventional plane wave path integral Monte Carlo results for helium fluid at low temperature.
conclusion: The proposed Brownian bridge construction is a valid and accurate approach for simulating quantum fluids with coherent states.
keywords: coherent state path integral Monte Carlo

title: The Scales Of Disorder In Perfect Quasicrystals
authors: Alan Rodrigo Mendoza Sosa, Atahualpa S. Kraemer, Michael Schmiedeberg, Erdal C. O\u{g}uz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical dichotomy between crystalline order and amorphous disorder is increasingly challenged by novel states that lack conventional crystalline symmetries while retaining crystal-like properties. Quasicrystals occupy a distinctive position within this expanding framework by possessing long-range order without translational periodicity, thereby permitting arbitrary [MATH]-fold rotational symmetry. Paradoxically, far from their unique symmetry center, high-symmetry quasicrystals closely resemble disordered patterns, raising the question of how deterministic order can be detected. Here we show that increasing rotational symmetry progressively suppresses local statistical signatures of quasiperiodicity, while preserving its underlying exact long-range order. This order is thus concealed below an emergent crossover length that grows linearly with [MATH]. Therefore, as [MATH], the disorder-like regime expands without bound, defining a symmetry-controlled geometric critical point at which deterministic order and randomness become statistically indistinguishable over any finite observation window. For finite [MATH], however, quasiperiodic order becomes detectable beyond this crossover, revealing a second emergent length scale that we identify as the size of a -- finite patches over which statistical properties recur despite the absence of conventional translational periodicity. In one dimension, the statistical-unit-cell size coincides with the crossover length, whereas in two dimensions it grows as [MATH], remaining smaller than the size of typical approximants and establishing a hierarchy of emergent length scales. Together, the disorder-to-order crossover and statistical unit cells provide a quantitative framework connecting crystals, quasicrystals, and amorphous matter, showing how apparent disorder can emerge from purely deterministic geometry.
tldr: This paper studies how increasing rotational symmetry in perfect quasicrystals suppresses local statistical signatures of quasiperiodicity, leading to an emergent crossover length beyond which deterministic order becomes indistinguishable from disorder.
motivation: Quasicrystals possess long-range order without translational periodicity, yet high-symmetry quasicrystals resemble disordered patterns, raising the question of how deterministic order can be detected.
method: The authors analyze the statistical properties of quasicrystals as a function of rotational symmetry, identifying a crossover length that scales linearly with the symmetry order, and define a statistical-unit-cell size that characterizes recurrence of statistical properties.
result: They show that as rotational symmetry increases, the disorder-like regime expands without bound, defining a symmetry-controlled geometric critical point where order and randomness become statistically indistinguishable over any finite observation window.
conclusion: The findings provide a quantitative framework connecting crystals, quasicrystals, and amorphous matter, showing how apparent disorder can emerge from purely deterministic geometry.

title: The Statistical Physics Of Unsaturated Soil Water: Kinetic Theory And Non Commutative Pore Water Dynamics
authors: Riccardo Rigon
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09416v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a statistical-mechanical theory of water in unsaturated soil whose outcome is a continuum field equation for the pore-occupancy g(r,x,t), the fraction of pores of radius r that are water-filled at position x and time t. The theory is built across three scales: microscopic inter-pore transfers set by Hagen-Poiseuille rates and a driving potential (the difference of pore-class chemical potentials, taken in capillary-gravitational form but open to adsorptive, osmotic, or thermal refinement); a mesoscale master equation relaxing the occupancy toward the equilibrium step g_eq=H(r*-r); and, on contracting the averaging volume to a point, the continuum balance d_t g + div F = C[g] - E - T, of which everything else is a limit, a moment, or a boundary resolution. The kinetic equation is an Onsager gradient flow descending the Gibbs free energy, with an H-theorem for the isothermal unforced system and mass conservation as its zeroth moment. A single dimensionless group, the pore-resolved Damkohler number Da(r,x), organizes the behavior and unifies phenomenologies long modelled separately. A Chapman-Enskog reduction identifies Richards' equation as the quasi-static (Da->0) limit, with matric potential and hydraulic conductivity K emerging only there and K vanishing below the percolation threshold; capillary-bundle and critical-path models are its diagonal and spectral limits. Hysteresis is the holonomy of a forcing bundle, a geometric phase rather than per-pore bistability, with a falsifiable loop-area law H ~ I^2. Preferential flow is what the same equation does where Da>1, so the Richards/preferential-flow dichotomy becomes a continuous Da-controlled crossover. Out of the quasi-static limit g(r) is the irreducible state variable. All inputs are geometric properties of the pore network, measurable from micro-CT and calibrated against no macroscopic data.
tldr: Develops a statistical-mechanical theory of water in unsaturated soil, deriving a continuum field equation for pore occupancy.
motivation: To provide a unified theoretical framework for unsaturated soil water dynamics that bridges microscopic pore-scale physics and macroscopic continuum models.
method: Builds a kinetic theory across three scales: microscopic inter-pore transfers, mesoscale master equation, and continuum balance equation, using Onsager gradient flow and Chapman-Enskog reduction.
result: Derives Richards' equation as a quasi-static limit, identifies hysteresis as a geometric phase, and shows preferential flow as a Damkohler-number-controlled crossover.
conclusion: The theory unifies various phenomenological models of unsaturated flow and provides a falsifiable framework based on pore network geometry.

title: Intrinsic Redundancy And Local Robustness In Finite $\beta$-Expansion Systems
authors: Miras Seilkhan Adilbek Taizhanov
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Redundancy in non-standard numeration systems is often associated with robustness, but its practical value in finite digital arithmetic depends on how representation, storage, and repair are defined. We study intrinsic redundancy in finite beta-expansion systems using a bounded-window model that separates semantic non-uniqueness from canonical codebook admissibility. The model distinguishes arithmetic canonicalization from corruption repair and evaluates structural detectability, value-preserving repair of the observed state, and survival of the original value. For the golden-ratio system and related multinacci bases, we prove that a genuine single-digit corruption in a canonically injective finite codebook cannot be semantically recovered by exact repair without external information. Semantic survival under exact structural repair is possible only for localized multi-digit perturbations corresponding to algebraic rewrite identities, such as the equivalence of 100 and 011. Experiments comparing standard binary, signed-digit non-adjacent form, and multinacci systems quantify trade-offs among codebook sparsity, fault visibility, canonicalization cost, residual error, and boundary loss. The results show that intrinsic beta-redundancy is a constrained-language resource for structural digital integrity rather than a substitute for classical error-control redundancy.
tldr: This paper studies redundancy in non-standard numeration systems (beta-expansions) using a bounded-window model, focusing on structural digital integrity rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand the practical value of intrinsic redundancy in finite beta-expansion systems for digital arithmetic, particularly regarding representation, storage, and repair.
method: The authors propose a bounded-window model that separates semantic non-uniqueness from canonical codebook admissibility, and analyze structural detectability, value-preserving repair, and survival of original value under single-digit corruptions.
result: For golden-ratio and multinacci bases, single-digit corruption in a canonically injective codebook cannot be semantically recovered without external information; semantic survival is only possible for localized multi-digit perturbations corresponding to algebraic rewrite identities.
conclusion: Intrinsic beta-redundancy is a constrained-language resource for structural digital integrity, not a substitute for classical error-control redundancy.

title: Geometric Planted Matchings In High Dimensions: The Power Of Multiple Views
authors: Timothy L. H. Wee, Kaylee Y. Yang, Zhou Fan, Cheng Mao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of recovering the correspondence between a collection of [MATH] points in [MATH] and a noisy, permuted version of those points. In the high-dimensional regime [MATH], under a Gaussian model with noise variance [MATH], prior work identifies [MATH] as the threshold for almost exact recovery. We prove that this threshold is all-or-nothing: for every fixed [MATH], no estimator recovers a positive fraction of the matching, and even estimating the matched point cloud in Euclidean distance is asymptotically no better than ignoring the correspondence. On the other hand, we consider a multi-view generalization of the problem where [MATH] noisy, independently permuted copies of the same latent point cloud are observed. Here we show that a simple polynomial-time procedure recovers all relative matchings up to [MATH] errors whenever [MATH]. Thus multiple views can break the impossibility barrier [MATH] for the original matching problem: in particular, for [MATH], the two-view model has no nontrivial recovery, but a third view makes all latent correspondences efficiently recoverable.
tldr: This paper studies the problem of recovering correspondences between noisy, permuted point clouds in high dimensions, and shows that multiple views can break the impossibility barrier for matching.
motivation: The problem of matching two point clouds under unknown permutation and noise is fundamental in statistics and machine learning, with applications in computer vision and data integration.
method: The authors analyze a Gaussian model with noise variance σ², prove an all-or-nothing threshold for single-view recovery, and propose a polynomial-time procedure for multi-view matching.
result: For a single view, no estimator can recover a positive fraction of the matching when σ² > 1. For multiple views, the procedure recovers all relative matchings up to o(1) errors whenever σ² < 1 + 1/(m-1) for m views.
conclusion: Multiple views can overcome the fundamental limitation of single-view matching, enabling efficient recovery even when individual views are too noisy.

title: Tests For Increasing Convex Ordering Based On Generalized Tsallis Entropy Measures
authors: Aritra Saha, Siddhartha Chakraborty, Md. Zafar Anis
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study several incomplete entropy measures, namely the Incomplete Weighted Cumulative Residual Entropy, the Incomplete Cumulative Residual Tsallis Entropy and its weighted version, and introduce the associated partial orderings. Their connections with certain well-known stochastic orderings are also investigated. Based on these characterizations, a class of nonparametric tests for stochastic equality against ordered alternatives is developed. The asymptotic properties of the proposed tests are derived, while their finite-sample performances are assessed through extensive Monte Carlo simulations under various alternative models and sample sizes. These tests are further compared with the test based on incomplete cumulative residual entropy proposed by Zardasht (2015).
tldr: This paper develops nonparametric tests for increasing convex ordering using generalized Tsallis entropy measures.
motivation: To provide statistical tests for stochastic ordering based on entropy measures, extending existing work on cumulative residual entropy.
method: The authors introduce incomplete weighted cumulative residual entropy and incomplete cumulative residual Tsallis entropy, derive associated partial orderings, and propose a class of nonparametric tests. Asymptotic properties are derived and finite-sample performance is evaluated via Monte Carlo simulations.
result: The proposed tests are shown to be consistent and outperform the existing test based on incomplete cumulative residual entropy in certain scenarios.
conclusion: The new entropy-based tests offer a useful tool for detecting increasing convex ordering in data.

title: Breaking Local-Minimum Traps In Spiking Neural Network-Based Solvers For CSPs Via Parallel Tempering
authors: Recep Bugra Uludag, Ahmet Efe, Ismail Akturk, Ulya R. Karpuzcu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) with stochastic neurons can solve constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) by encoding constraints via connectivity and performing probabilistic search via spike dynamics. However, fixed-temperature stochastic dynamics often get trapped in local minima - near-satisfying configurations - a vulnerability that escalates with problem difficulty. To overcome this, we integrate parallel tempering (PT) into the neural sampling solver, running multiple parallel replicas at varying inverse temperatures. Replicas periodically exchange temperatures rather than network states, managing the trade-off between exploration and concentration around low-energy configurations while preserving asynchronous, spike-based computation. We evaluate this architecture against a parallel baseline of four independent, fixed-temperature solvers using equal computational resources across 1000 instances from the SATLIB uf20-91 benchmark. Parallel tempering improves success probability on 332 instances while worsening only 5. Crucially, these gains are concentrated on hard instances where independent solvers fail. Violation trajectory analysis confirms the underlying mechanism: temperature exchanges allow replicas to traverse energy barriers unreachable by fixed-temperature dynamics, successfully escaping the narrow basins that constrain the baseline. To our knowledge, this represents the first integration of parallel tempering into an SNN-based CSP solver.
tldr: This paper integrates parallel tempering into spiking neural network-based solvers for constraint satisfaction problems to escape local minima.
motivation: Fixed-temperature stochastic dynamics in SNN-based CSP solvers often get trapped in local minima, especially for hard instances.
method: The authors run multiple parallel replicas at varying inverse temperatures and periodically exchange temperatures between replicas, preserving asynchronous spike-based computation.
result: On the SATLIB uf20-91 benchmark, parallel tempering improves success probability on 332 out of 1000 instances while worsening only 5, with gains concentrated on hard instances.
conclusion: Temperature exchanges allow replicas to traverse energy barriers unreachable by fixed-temperature dynamics, successfully escaping local minima.

title: Federated Learning Architecture: Data Privacy And System Security Approaches
authors: Cagdas Karatas, Hibanur Karadogan, Ahmet Yasin Ertug, Busra Buyuktanir, Kazim Yildiz, Gozde Karatas Baydogmus
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study explores the integration of homomorphic encryption and differential privacy techniques to enhance data privacy and security in Federated Learning (FL) systems. FL allows data to remain on local devices, eliminating the need for centralized data collection; however, sensitive information may still be leaked during model updates. To address this issue, homomorphic encryption enables computations on encrypted data, while differential privacy prevents the extraction of individual information through statistical techniques applied to model outputs. The proposed architecture was tested on the Framingham, Pima Indians Diabetes, and Bank Marketing datasets, revealing that enhanced privacy can be achieved without significantly compromising model accuracy. Furthermore, the impact of data heterogeneity among clients on model performance was analyzed, and it was concluded that strategies such as the careful selection of differential privacy parameters and training settings, along with the use of larger datasets, can improve the efficiency of FL. The findings demonstrate that privacy-preserving and high-performance artificial intelligence systems can be securely applied in sensitive domains such as healthcare and finance.
tldr: This paper proposes a federated learning architecture combining homomorphic encryption and differential privacy to enhance data privacy and security.
motivation: Federated learning still risks leaking sensitive information from model updates; the authors aim to mitigate this by integrating privacy-preserving techniques.
method: The architecture uses homomorphic encryption for computations on encrypted data and differential privacy to prevent individual information extraction, tested on three datasets.
result: Enhanced privacy is achieved without significantly compromising model accuracy; data heterogeneity impacts performance, but careful parameter selection and larger datasets improve efficiency.
conclusion: Privacy-preserving and high-performance AI systems can be securely applied in sensitive domains like healthcare and finance.

title: SolarChain-Eval: A Physics-Constrained Benchmark For Trustworthy Economic Agents In Decentralized Energy Markets
authors: Shilin Ou, Yifan Xu, Luyao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08681v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As agentic AI systems are increasingly applied to cyber-physical environments, their evaluation requires assessment of both task performance and trustworthiness. In decentralized energy markets, autonomous agents may improve market utility, but may also exploit invalid physical data, create artificial liquidity, and produce unstable governance decisions. Therefore, we propose SolarChain-Eval, a physics-constrained benchmark for evaluating trustworthy economic agents. It formulates market governance as a Gymnasium-compatible Markov Decision Process, where agents make hourly decisions. SolarChain-Eval evaluates each policy across multiple dimensions, including market utility, physical safety, slippage, action smoothness, spatial fairness, and auditability. To support agentic evaluation, SolarChain-Eval incorporates an LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer. The Planner defines episode-level action bounds and audit rules, while the Auditor reviews and revises high-risk actions. All interventions are recorded through structured logs, including trigger signals, proposed actions, revised actions, and audit rationales. Experiments with static, random, myopic, RL, and RL+LLM policies reveal a clear utility-safety trade-off. RL agents improve market utility but can still produce unsafe behavior. When the physics penalty is removed, reward-maximizing agents exploit invalid generation and increase artificial liquidity. The LLM Planner/Auditor improves auditability and mitigates selected risks, but it cannot fully compensate for a misspecified reward function. These results indicate that trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires both physical constraints and transparent intervention traces. We release data and code as open access on GitHub for replicability.
tldr: A benchmark for evaluating trustworthy economic agents in decentralized energy markets using physics constraints and LLM-based auditing.
motivation: Autonomous agents in decentralized energy markets may exploit invalid data or create artificial liquidity, so a benchmark is needed to evaluate both task performance and trustworthiness.
method: The benchmark formulates market governance as a Markov Decision Process, includes an LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer, and evaluates policies across dimensions like market utility, physical safety, and auditability.
result: Experiments show a utility-safety trade-off; RL agents improve utility but can produce unsafe behavior, and the LLM Planner/Auditor mitigates some risks but cannot fully compensate for misspecified reward functions.
conclusion: Trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires both physical constraints and transparent intervention traces.

title: A Unified Approach To Interpreting Knowledge Distillation For Large Language Models Via Interactions
authors: Qingzhuo Wang, Ruiyang Qin, Zhenxin Qin, Wen Shen, Zhihua Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Despite the success of knowledge distillation (KD) in Large Language Models (LLMs), the underlying mechanism behind its efficacy remains unclear. In this paper, we propose a unified approach to explore the common mechanism of various KD methods using interactions. Specifically, we decompose the output score of the LLM into the sum of numerous interactions. Each interaction represents a nonlinear relationship involving a set of input variables (e.g., words). Based on the decomposed interactions, we discover that the common mechanism underlying various KD methods is the sparsification of interactions, i.e., student models retain fewer interactions for inference while suppressing other interactions to zero effects. Furthermore, we discover that the performance variance across different KD methods arises from their capabilities in handling complex interactions. A KD method typically yields better performance if it enables the student model to achieve higher sparsity of complex interactions. Motivated by these insights, we propose a plug-and-play loss function called Complex Interaction Penalty (CIP) to explicitly enforce the sparsity of complex interactions during the distillation process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that integrating CIP consistently improves the performance of diverse KD methods on both in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
tldr: This paper proposes a unified approach to interpret knowledge distillation in large language models using interactions, and introduces a loss function to improve distillation performance.
motivation: The mechanism behind knowledge distillation in LLMs is unclear; the authors aim to uncover a common mechanism across different KD methods.
method: They decompose the output score into interactions representing nonlinear relationships among input variables, and propose a Complex Interaction Penalty (CIP) loss to enforce sparsity of complex interactions.
result: Experiments show that CIP consistently improves performance of various KD methods on in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
conclusion: The common mechanism of KD is sparsification of interactions, and explicitly enforcing sparsity of complex interactions enhances distillation.
