conclusion: The study provides insights into nonequilibrium precipitate patterns but does not relate to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Ghost Mechanism: An Analytical Model Of Abrupt Learning In Recurrent Networks
authors: Fatih Dinc, Ege Cirakman, Bariscan Kurtkaya, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yiqi Jiang, Mark J. Schnitzer, And Hidenori Tanaka
abstract:
Author(s): Fatih Dinc, Ege Cirakman, Bariscan Kurtkaya, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yiqi Jiang, Mark J. Schnitzer, and Hidenori Tanaka

This study establishes the ghost mechanism as an underlying mechanism for abrupt learning, whereby the recurrent neural network develops ghost points—transient dynamical bottlenecks—and identifies ways to overcome the training instabilities.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021058] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a ghost mechanism to explain abrupt learning in recurrent neural networks, focusing on dynamical systems and machine learning theory.
motivation: Understanding abrupt learning phenomena in recurrent networks is important for training stability and performance.
method: The authors develop an analytical model of ghost points as transient dynamical bottlenecks in recurrent neural networks.
result: They identify ghost points as a key mechanism underlying abrupt learning and propose ways to overcome training instabilities.
conclusion: The ghost mechanism provides a theoretical framework for abrupt learning in recurrent networks, with implications for improving training.

title: Three-Dimensional Xy Universality And Nonlinear Magnetic Susceptibility In A Kagome Ice Compound
authors: Kan Zhao, Hao Deng, Hua Chen, Nvsen Ma, Noah Oefele, Jiesen Guo, Xueling Cui, Chen Tang, Matthias J. Gutmann, Thomas Mueller, Yixi Su, Vladimir Hutanu, Changqing Jin, And Philipp Gegenwart
abstract:
Author(s): Kan Zhao, Hao Deng, Hua Chen, Nvsen Ma, Noah Oefele, Jiesen Guo, Xueling Cui, Chen Tang, Matthias J. Gutmann, Thomas Mueller, Yixi Su, Vladimir Hutanu, Changqing Jin, and Philipp Gegenwart

Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in the kagome spin ice HoAgGe reveal hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground states, reached via a three-dimensional XY universality class transition.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021043] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in a kagome spin ice compound, revealing a three-dimensional XY universality class transition and hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking.
motivation: To investigate the nature of the ground state and phase transition in the kagome spin ice HoAgGe, which exhibits a three-dimensional XY universality class.
method: Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements were performed on single crystals of HoAgGe, combined with neutron scattering and other techniques.
result: The measurements reveal hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground state and a transition belonging to the three-dimensional XY universality class.
conclusion: The study provides experimental evidence for a three-dimensional XY transition and hidden order in a kagome spin ice, relevant to frustrated magnetism.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: This review covers atomic-scale microscopy techniques for measuring disorder in semiconductors, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding atomic-scale disorder is crucial for semiconductor material properties, but the paper focuses on materials characterization rather than quantum information processing.
method: The review discusses three real-space techniques: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, applied to compound semiconductors.
result: The paper emphasizes combined use of these probes to achieve a more complete picture of defects, but does not present quantum information or thermodynamic results.
conclusion: The work is purely materials science and does not align with any of the specified research directions.

title: Gravitational And Other Shifts Of Whispering-gallery And Gravitational State Interference Patterns Of Light Neutral Particles
authors: V V Nesvizhevsky, J A Pioquinto, K Schreiner, S Baeßler, P Crivelli, F Nez, S Reynaud, P Yzombard, S A Vasiliev And E Widmann
abstract: We discuss the interference patterns of gravitational and whispering gallery quantum states that can be observed with neutrons, atoms, antiatoms, muonium (Mu), positronium (Ps), and other light neutral particles. A gravitational shift of interference patterns of neutron gravitational and whispering-gallery states can be easily observed with cold, very cold, or ultracold neutrons. The developed methods can be used for observing/searching for other shifts in fundamental neutron physics experiments, for instance, for measuring the gravitational constant or constraining the neutron electric charge. A series of such measurements will be made with neutrons at the PF1B, PF2, D17 facilities at the ILL. A peculiar feature of analogous atomic (anti-atomic) experiments is the much smaller effective critical energies of the materials of mirrors for (anti)atoms. We evaluated parameters that make a measurement of the hydrogen and antihydrogen whispering-gallery states and their gravitational shifts feasible. A series of such measurements will be made with hydrogen and deuterium atoms by the GRASIAN collaboration in Vienna and Turku. A similar measurement with antihydrogen atoms may be of interest for the GBAR experiment, the ASACUSA experiment, which is producing a beam of slow antihydrogen atoms, and other experiments at CERN that study the gravitational properties of antimatter. Quantum reflection (QR) of Mu and Ps from material surfaces opens the possibility of observing whispering-gallery states, although such measurements remain experimentally challenging. Because of the small masses of Mu and Ps, their effective critical energies of the mirror materials are much higher for them than the effective critical energies for hydrogen and other atoms. The observation of gravitational shifts of such states is particularly demanding because of the extremely short lifetimes of these systems. Measurements of whispering gallery states with all these atoms and particles yield precise and detailed information on the QR properties of materials, providing valuable input for both fundamental physics and surface physics studies.
tldr: This paper discusses gravitational and whispering gallery state interference patterns for light neutral particles, focusing on experimental measurements of gravitational shifts and quantum reflection.
motivation: To explore gravitational and other shifts in interference patterns of quantum states of neutrons, atoms, and antiatoms, which could provide tests of fundamental physics and surface properties.
method: The authors analyze the feasibility of observing gravitational and whispering gallery states for various particles (neutrons, hydrogen, antihydrogen, muonium, positronium) using existing and proposed experimental setups.
result: They find that gravitational shifts can be observed with neutrons, and similar measurements with hydrogen and antihydrogen are feasible; muonium and positronium experiments are more challenging due to short lifetimes.
conclusion: These measurements can yield precise information on quantum reflection properties and fundamental constants, but the work is primarily experimental and phenomenological, not advancing quantum information or thermodynamics theory.

title: Inferring The Underlying Higher-order Network Structure From Low-resolution Interaction State Data
authors: Chuang Ma, Xiao-Feng Luo, Rui-Hui He, Dao-Yu Li, Hai-Feng Zhang And Gui-Quan Sun
abstract: Network reconstruction aims to infer the underlying interactions between entities from observed data and serves as a cornerstone of network science. While most existing methods focus on dynamics-based data and primarily target binary interactions, real-world data often reflect coarse-grained interaction states of individuals over specific time intervals and may involve complex multi-body interactions beyond pairwise connections. Reconstructing the underlying higher-order network structure from such low-resolution interaction state data is therefore of critical importance. In this paper, we formulate an optimization model for inferring higher-order structures based on the minimum description length principle. To solve this problem, we propose a Bayesian network reconstruction method that integrates distribution estimation with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Our method begins by generating candidate configurations for each time interval via MCMC sampling, then constructs a Bayesian network—guided by minimum-entropy—to capture dependencies between configurations across different time intervals. Finally, an iterative update strategy based on distribution estimation is employed to approach the optimal solution. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.
tldr: This paper proposes a Bayesian method to infer higher-order network structures from low-resolution interaction state data using minimum description length and MCMC sampling.
motivation: Existing network reconstruction methods focus on binary interactions and dynamics-based data, but real-world data often involve coarse-grained interaction states and multi-body interactions.
method: The method uses MCMC sampling to generate candidate configurations per time interval, builds a Bayesian network guided by minimum-entropy to capture dependencies, and iteratively updates via distribution estimation.
result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness and robustness in reconstructing higher-order network structures.
conclusion: The proposed approach successfully infers underlying higher-order interactions from low-resolution data, addressing a gap in network reconstruction.

title: Characterizing The Low Energy Breakdown In Interpreting Photoionization Delays
authors: Brock Grafstrom And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: Typical attosecond pump–probe experiments utilize a combination of extreme ultraviolet and IR laser pulses to extract precise timing information of electron dynamics. For sufficiently high photoelectron energies it is typically assumed that Wigner and Coulomb–laser-coupling (CLC) delays are separable, adding up to the experimentally measured photoionization delay. However, no widespread consensus has been reached on how to best interpret time delays at low photoelectron energies or IR wavelengths shorter than 800 nm. These questions are becoming crucial for the interpretation of state of the art ultrafast experiments in atoms and molecules studying electronic motion in bound and quasi-resonant states, where the dynamics of interest are typically only present within the low-energy portion of time delay spectra. In this work we provide an analytical cut-off law which describes the minimum energy where it is valid to approximate the total delay as the sum of the Wigner and CLC components for a given probe laser frequency. In doing so, we discover that the breakdown between the short-range (Wigner) and long-range (CLC) delay components begins around 23 eV for IR wavelengths near 400 nm. This energy is markedly higher than what is traditionally assumed, and therefore has important implications for interpretation of photoionization delay experiments probed with visible light.
tldr: This paper studies photoionization delays in attosecond pump-probe experiments, focusing on the breakdown of the separability of Wigner and Coulomb-laser-coupling delays at low photoelectron energies.
motivation: Interpreting time delays in ultrafast experiments is crucial for studying electronic motion in bound and quasi-resonant states, but no consensus exists for low photoelectron energies or short IR wavelengths.
method: The authors derive an analytical cut-off law that determines the minimum energy where the total delay can be approximated as the sum of Wigner and CLC components, and apply it to various probe laser frequencies.
result: The breakdown between short-range and long-range delay components begins around 23 eV for IR wavelengths near 400 nm, which is higher than traditionally assumed.
conclusion: The findings have important implications for interpreting photoionization delay experiments probed with visible light, especially at low energies.

title: Distinct Phenomenon On Chaos Synchrony: Chirality
authors: Gualberto C. Solís-Perales And Ricardo Femat
abstract:
Author(s): Gualberto C. Solís-Perales and Ricardo Femat

Among others, chirality is a property of organometallic molecules whose main feature is that the spatial superposition is exclusively observed through a specular plane. A specular plane is a physical kind of subspace onto which chiral objects can already be superposed. That is, chirality corresponds…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014206] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies chirality in the context of chaos synchrony, a topic unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Chirality is a property of molecules where spatial superposition is observed through a specular plane; the authors investigate this phenomenon in chaotic systems.
method: The paper likely uses dynamical systems theory and synchronization analysis to study chirality in chaotic systems.
result: The paper reports a distinct phenomenon of chirality in chaos synchrony.
conclusion: The findings contribute to the understanding of chirality in nonlinear dynamics but have no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Sequential Multi-Step Nanoimprint Lithography Fabrication Of Zero-Mode Waveguide Nanoaperture Arrays To Enhance Single Molecule Fluorescence Detection
authors: Hamza Khelidj, Badre Kerzabi, Igor Ozerov, Olivier Hector, David Grosso, J\'er\^ome Wenger
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Zero-mode waveguides (ZMWs) enable single-molecule fluorescence detection at micromolar concentrations by confining light to nanoscale volumes, overcoming the diffraction limit of confocal microscopy. However, their widespread adoption is hindered by high fabrication costs and limited throughput of traditional methods like focused ion beam or electron-beam lithography. Here, we introduce a scalable cost-effective approach using sequential nanoimprint lithography (NIL) combined with hydrofluoric acid etching to fabricate ZMW arrays with tunable diameters from a single initial master. In our sequential nanoimprint approach, each stamped NIL output serves as a master for the next nanoimprint generation. By leveraging the shrinkage of sol-gel nanopatterns during annealing, we achieve a cumulative diameter reduction from 230 nm to 115 nm over four successive imprints, all based on the same initial master. The resulting ZMWs exhibit detection volumes reduced by up to 1000-fold and fluorescence enhancement exceeding 16x, achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art focused ion beam-fabricated devices. Eliminating the need for multiple master structures significantly expands the scalability of nanoimprint lithography approaches. By lowering the nanofabrication barriers and making ZMW arrays more accessible, the sequential NIL method paves the way towards broader adoption of nanophotonic devices in single-molecule biophysics, biosensing, and surface patterning applications.
tldr: This paper presents a scalable nanoimprint lithography method to fabricate zero-mode waveguide arrays for single-molecule fluorescence detection.
motivation: Zero-mode waveguides enable single-molecule detection at high concentrations but are costly to fabricate; the authors aim to reduce cost and increase throughput.
method: Sequential nanoimprint lithography using sol-gel shrinkage to reduce aperture diameter from 230 nm to 115 nm over four generations.
result: Detection volumes reduced up to 1000-fold and fluorescence enhancement exceeding 16x, comparable to focused ion beam devices.
conclusion: The sequential NIL method lowers fabrication barriers and makes ZMW arrays more accessible for biophysics and biosensing.

title: Co-design Approach To Aperture Masking For Imaging Through Atmospheric Turbulence
authors: Olivier Herscovici-Schiller, Laurent M. Mugnier, Alice Fontbonne, Pauline Trouv\'e-Peloux, Fr\'ed\'eric Champagnat, Yann Lucas, Yann Lai-Tim, Fr\'ed\'eric Cassaing
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aperture masking interferometry is a technique originally designed to alleviate the influence of atmospheric turbulence on images recorded on ground-based telescopes. In this communication, we explore the optimization of the aperture mask by an optical/digital co-design approach in order to obtain diffraction-limited images of relatively bright objects imaged through turbulence. We show that, with a few simplifying assumptions, it is possible to express the Mean Square Error of the restored image as a function of the chosen mask, of the spatial Power Spectral Density of the observed object and of the noise level, without actually computing any image. This allows us to optimize the aperture mask with a reduced computing cost. We also implement a multi-frame myopic algorithm to estimate jointly the observed object, the piston and the tip-tilt in front of each sub-aperture, and check by simulations that the aperture masks obtained indeed allow a satisfactory image reconstruction.
tldr: This paper presents an optical/digital co-design approach to optimize aperture masks for imaging through atmospheric turbulence, aiming to achieve diffraction-limited images.
motivation: Atmospheric turbulence degrades images from ground-based telescopes; aperture masking interferometry can mitigate this, but mask design is typically heuristic. The authors aim to optimize the mask using a co-design approach.
method: The mean square error of the restored image is expressed as a function of the mask, object power spectral density, and noise level, enabling optimization without full image computation. A multi-frame myopic algorithm jointly estimates the object and wavefront aberrations.
result: Simulations show that the optimized aperture masks enable satisfactory image reconstruction.
conclusion: The co-design approach reduces computational cost and yields effective masks for turbulence mitigation.

title: Optical Fourier Surfaces For Free-Space Computer-Generated Holography
authors: Y. M. Glauser, C. -Y. Shen, D. B. Seda, \c{c}. I\c{s}il, P. Benito Eberhard, H. Niese, J. G. Crimmann, D. Petter, G. Nagamine, S. J. W. Vonk, N. Lassaline, A. Ozcan, D. J. Norris
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-generated holography can shape electromagnetic fields by encoding wavefront information in nanostructured surfaces. However, despite significant progress, hologram designs for visible and near-infrared wavelengths remain largely limited by fabrication constraints. Most implementations rely on lithographic methods that produce discretized surfaces that do not match the wave nature of light. Further advances would benefit from accurate continuous (grayscale) control of interfacial profiles, which would allow straightforward design principles from Fourier optics to be applied. In this work, we introduce optical Fourier surfaces as a versatile, intuitive platform for free-space computer-generated holograms. Exploiting these arbitrarily wavy surfaces, we demonstrate three different design strategies for computer-generated holography. First, we use an analytical linear design approach based on sinusoidal lenses and gratings as fundamental holographic building blocks. Second, we enhance diffraction efficiencies through an iterative Fourier-transform algorithm. Finally, we extend our framework with machine-learning-based inverse design, creating wavelength-multiplexed holograms that reconstruct distinct diffraction responses in a predefined image plane. Our results combine advanced thermal scanning-probe lithography with flexible design strategies to create useful structures for photonic applications, particularly in settings where rapid prototyping is crucial.
tldr: This paper introduces optical Fourier surfaces for free-space computer-generated holography, focusing on fabrication and design strategies for visible and near-infrared wavelengths.
motivation: Current hologram designs are limited by fabrication constraints that produce discretized surfaces, and the authors aim to achieve accurate continuous control of interfacial profiles to apply Fourier optics principles.
method: The authors use thermal scanning-probe lithography to create arbitrarily wavy surfaces and demonstrate three design strategies: analytical linear design, iterative Fourier-transform algorithm, and machine-learning-based inverse design.
result: They demonstrate wavelength-multiplexed holograms that reconstruct distinct diffraction responses, combining advanced fabrication with flexible design strategies.
conclusion: Optical Fourier surfaces provide a versatile platform for computer-generated holography, particularly useful for rapid prototyping in photonic applications.

title: Scale-Bridging Phase-Field Modeling Of Microstructure Evolution By Fe$^2$ Computational Homogenization
authors: Geralf H\"utter, Fenil Lathiya, Vincent von Oertzen, Bjoern Kiefer
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phase-field models have become a standard tool for simulating complex microstructure evolution in materials, but their application to engineering-scale components is often hindered by prohibitive computational costs arising from the need to resolve fine-scale features. To address this challenge, we propose a consistent homogenization framework for phase-field theory. By enforcing a Hill-Mandel-type condition of micro-homogeneity formulated in terms of Gurtin's microforces, a well-posed boundary value problem is derived for the representative volume element (RVE), establishing rigorous micro-macro relations for both the order parameter and its gradient. The theory is implemented within a computational two-scale (FE[MATH]) scheme and validated against direct numerical simulations. Two distinct examples are investigated: a minimal Allen-Cahn model and a mechanically-coupled model for stress-driven martensitic phase transformation. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can reliably predict the spatial and temporal evolution of the macroscopically averaged fields with reasonable accuracy.
tldr: This paper proposes a computational homogenization framework for phase-field modeling of microstructure evolution, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Phase-field models are computationally expensive for engineering-scale components due to fine-scale resolution requirements. The authors aim to develop a consistent homogenization framework to bridge scales.
method: A Hill-Mandel-type micro-homogeneity condition is enforced using Gurtin's microforces, leading to a well-posed RVE boundary value problem. The theory is implemented in a computational two-scale FE² scheme.
result: The framework is validated on a minimal Allen-Cahn model and a mechanically-coupled martensitic phase transformation model, showing reliable prediction of macroscopically averaged fields.
conclusion: The proposed homogenization approach enables efficient phase-field simulations at engineering scales while maintaining accuracy for microstructure evolution.

title: Wireless Decentralized Federated Learning Via Device Clustering And Inter-Cluster Link Enhancement
authors: William Weijia Zheng, Hang Liu, Ying-Jun Angela Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) dispenses with the central server of classical FL by utilizing peer-to-peer model exchanges among edge devices. This server-free architecture enables ad-hoc, flexible distributed learning in large device-to-device (D2D) networks. However, wireless DFL converges slowly because peer-to-peer model aggregation incurs high delays and errors. Each DFL training round involves many-to-many gradient sharing over wireless channels, resulting in uncoordinated channel access, large communication errors from stragglers, and slow model consensus, especially in large-scale D2D networks with pronounced clustering structures. We address these aggregation bottlenecks by provisioning a few reliable backhaul links at straggling nodes to enhance network connectivity. Building on this idea, our budget-aware, cluster-centric DFL framework first partitions the network into densely connected clusters, and then allocates the limited backhaul budget to selected cluster heads. The resulting two-tier protocol executes fast, parallel model aggregation within clusters and infrequent inter-cluster exchanges among the heads, yielding an O(1/t) convergence rate in t iterations. Numerical experiments on image-classification tasks confirm that our approach accelerates convergence compared to state-of-the-art DFL baselines with only a few strategically placed backhaul links.
tldr: This paper proposes a wireless decentralized federated learning framework using device clustering and limited backhaul links to accelerate convergence.
motivation: Wireless DFL suffers from slow convergence due to high delays and errors in peer-to-peer model aggregation, especially in large-scale networks with clustering structures.
method: The framework partitions the network into densely connected clusters and allocates a limited backhaul budget to selected cluster heads, enabling fast intra-cluster aggregation and infrequent inter-cluster exchanges.
result: The proposed approach achieves an O(1/t) convergence rate and accelerates convergence on image-classification tasks compared to state-of-the-art DFL baselines.
conclusion: Strategically placing a few backhaul links can significantly improve wireless DFL performance without requiring full connectivity.

title: An Explicit Higher-Order Dual Basis For A Multiplicatively Calder\'on Preconditioned Electric Field Integral Equation
authors: Bernd Hofmann, Thomas F. Eibert, Francesco P. Andriulli, Simon B. Adrian
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One of the most effective means to precondition the electric field integral equation (EFIE) discretized with Rao-Wilton-Glisson (RWG) functions is the multiplicative Calder\'on preconditioner employing Buffa-Christiansen (BC) functions as a basis dual to the RWG basis. It results in a formulation that is free from the dense-discretization and the low-frequency breakdown. To generalize the multiplicative Calder\'on preconditioner from the low-order BC and RWG basis to higher orders, we utilize B-spline-based basis functions and establish the first explicit high-order dual basis. It can be regarded as a generalization of the BC functions to arbitrary polynomial degrees and constitutes a fundamental building block for other approaches that rely on a dual basis. Numerical results for the obtained preconditioner demonstrate a low and constant number of generalized minimum residual (GMRES) iterations independent of the number of unknonws and the polynomial degree for canonical and realistic perfectly electrically conducting (PEC) scatterers; a key to enable the full potential of higher-order bases.
tldr: This paper presents a higher-order dual basis for the multiplicative Calderón preconditioner applied to the electric field integral equation, improving numerical stability for electromagnetic scattering problems.
motivation: The multiplicative Calderón preconditioner for the EFIE is limited to low-order basis functions; a higher-order dual basis is needed to extend its benefits to higher-order discretizations.
method: The authors construct an explicit higher-order dual basis using B-spline functions, generalizing the Buffa-Christiansen basis to arbitrary polynomial degrees, and integrate it into the multiplicative Calderón preconditioner.
result: Numerical experiments show that the preconditioner achieves a low and constant number of GMRES iterations independent of the number of unknowns and polynomial degree for canonical and realistic PEC scatterers.
conclusion: The proposed higher-order dual basis enables the full potential of higher-order bases in Calderón preconditioning, offering a robust solver for electromagnetic integral equations.

title: Another Look At The Static Pde Approach To Multidimensional Extrapolation
authors: Hwi Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a variant of the static PDE based extrapolation method (2014 Aslam, SIAM J. Sci. Comp) for extending smooth fields across interfaces implicitly defined as zero level sets. Our approach introduces the idea of relaxed upwinding finite differences as a key modification within the fast sweeping method. Unlike existing approaches, we require function values and their normal derivatives only on the first grid layer inside the domain adjacent to the boundary, thereby improving computational efficiency and flexibility. To further improve accuracy, we introduce a simple boundary reconstruction technique that significantly reduces the numerical error in the extrapolated solution near the boundary. Numerical experiments indicate enhanced performance of our approach across a range of domain geometries, including those with high curvature features.
tldr: This paper presents a variant of the static PDE-based extrapolation method for extending smooth fields across interfaces, using relaxed upwinding finite differences and a boundary reconstruction technique.
motivation: Existing static PDE extrapolation methods require function values and normal derivatives on multiple grid layers, which can be computationally inefficient and less flexible.
method: The authors introduce relaxed upwinding finite differences within the fast sweeping method, requiring data only on the first grid layer, and add a boundary reconstruction technique to reduce numerical error.
result: Numerical experiments show improved performance across various domain geometries, including those with high curvature features.
conclusion: The proposed variant enhances computational efficiency and accuracy for extrapolating smooth fields across implicitly defined interfaces.

title: Continuous Aperture Array-Assisted Integrated Communication And Navigation In Leo Satellite Constellations
authors: Qi Wang, Xiaoming Chen, Qiao Qi, Zhaolin Wang, Yuanwei Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a novel continuous aperture array (CAPA)-assisted integrated communication and navigation (ICAN) framework for low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations. Within this framework, an electromagnetic-based collaborative transmission model is developed, in which multiple satellites equipped with CAPAs simultaneously radiate downlink data streams and navigation reference signals over shared spectrum. Building upon this, the achievable communication rate and the navigation Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) are derived, which explicitly characterize the intrinsic coupling between the dual-function beamformers and system performance. To improve the positioning accuracy with communication quality of service guarantee, a joint beamforming optimization problem is formulated to minimize the average CRB subject to transmit power budgets and minimum rate constraints. To tackle the inherent infinite-dimensionality of the CAPA beamformer design, an ICAN channel subspace is introduced to equivalently transform the formulation into a tractable finite-dimensional problem, which is then efficiently solved via an iterative convex optimization algorithm. Finally, numerical results demonstrate that the proposed CAPA-assisted beamforming design algorithm significantly outperforms conventional discrete phased array architectures and other benchmark schemes, yielding notable improvements in ICAN performance.
tldr: This paper proposes a continuous aperture array (CAPA)-assisted integrated communication and navigation framework for LEO satellite constellations, focusing on joint beamforming optimization to improve positioning accuracy under communication constraints.
motivation: To enhance both communication and navigation performance in LEO satellite systems by leveraging CAPA technology, which offers higher degrees of freedom than conventional phased arrays.
method: An electromagnetic-based collaborative transmission model is developed, and a joint beamforming optimization problem is formulated to minimize the average Cramer-Rao bound subject to power and rate constraints. The infinite-dimensional problem is transformed into a finite-dimensional one using an ICAN channel subspace and solved via iterative convex optimization.
result: Numerical results show that the proposed CAPA-assisted beamforming design significantly outperforms conventional discrete phased array architectures and other benchmarks in integrated communication and navigation performance.
conclusion: CAPA technology can substantially improve the trade-off between communication and navigation in LEO satellite constellations, offering a promising approach for future satellite systems.

title: Modeling And Analysis For Multiple-Layer Leo Satellite Internet Of Things Constellations
authors: Ming Ying, Xiaoming Chen, Qiao Qi, Yichao Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To provide multiple-satellite coverage for global Internet of Things (IoT), a low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite IoT constellation usually contains multiple-layer orbits with different altitudes. However, the performance of multiple-layer LEO satellite IoT constellations under practical Rician fading satellite channels remains unknown due to complex theoretical modeling and intractable mathematical analysis. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a stochastic geometry-based modeling and analysis framework for multiple-layer LEO satellite IoT constellations, integrating Rician channel modeling and Cox point processes. Specifically, we introduce a novel channel approximation method to overcome the intractable expressions caused by the Rician fading. Building on this method, we derive exact closed-form expressions for key performance metrics, including connectivity probability, coverage probability, and transmission rate, especially in the case of IoT short-packet transmission. Extensive simulation results validate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed model and reveal significant design insights. The results not only provide new theoretical perspectives for modeling and analysis of LEO satellite IoT constellations but also offer practical guidance for system deployment and optimization.
tldr: This paper proposes a stochastic geometry-based framework for modeling and analyzing multiple-layer LEO satellite IoT constellations under Rician fading channels.
motivation: The performance of multiple-layer LEO satellite IoT constellations under practical Rician fading is unknown due to complex modeling and analysis challenges.
method: The authors introduce a novel channel approximation method and derive closed-form expressions for connectivity, coverage, and transmission rate using Cox point processes.
result: Exact closed-form expressions for key performance metrics are derived and validated through simulations, revealing design insights for system deployment.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides new theoretical perspectives and practical guidance for LEO satellite IoT constellation design and optimization.

title: Nonexchangeable Logit Dynamics With Cost Constraints: Different Viewpoints And Numerical Analysis
authors: Tomohiro Tanaka Hidekazu Yoshioka
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09106v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The logit dynamic, a nonlinear dynamical system, subject to a const constraint with heterogeneous agents is formulated, and its well-posedness is studied from both agent-based (stochastic differential equation: SDE) and probabilistic (Fokker-Planck equation: FPE) viewpoints. The state space of agent actions is a compact domain in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. The SDE is of the McKean-Vlasov type and is driven by jumps with finite variations, whereas the FPE is a nonlinear integro-differential equation. A key to our mathematical analysis of the FPE is adding a regularization factor into the cost constraint to mitigate the blow-up of the logit function. This property carries over to the McKean-Vlasov SDE. We also present a numerical method based on a na\"ive finite difference discretization for computing the FPE along with demonstrative computational examples, showing that the regularization method does not critically affect numerical solutions while preventing the breakdown of numerical computation. Finally, we conduct another demonstrative application study in which environmental, energy, and fishery resources intersect.
tldr: This paper studies logit dynamics with cost constraints from agent-based and probabilistic viewpoints, with numerical analysis.
motivation: To formulate and analyze a logit dynamic system with heterogeneous agents under cost constraints, ensuring well-posedness and numerical stability.
method: Uses McKean-Vlasov SDE with jumps and a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation with a regularization factor to prevent blow-up, along with finite difference discretization.
result: The regularization method prevents numerical breakdown without critically affecting solutions; demonstrative examples in environmental, energy, and fishery resources are provided.
conclusion: The proposed regularization approach effectively stabilizes the logit dynamics model, enabling numerical computation for applications in resource management.

title: A Stabilizer Interpretation Of The Grothendieck-Teichm\"uller Group $\mathsf{GRT}_1(\mathbf K)$
authors: Hidekazu Furusho Benjamin Enriquez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: If [MATH] and [MATH] are Lie algebras, then the product [MATH] of their outer automorphism groups naturally acts on the set of outer Lie algebra morphisms from [MATH] to [MATH]; the stabilizer of the outer class of a given such morphism is then a subgroup of [MATH]. We show that this leads to two related interpretation of the Grothendieck-Teichm\"uller group [MATH], where [MATH] are the Lie algebra of infinitesimal braids on the plane (resp. framed infinitesimal braids on the sphere) with 3 and 4 (resp. 4 and 5) strands: namely, it can be expressed as the joint intersection of the stabilizer groups of the outer classes of certain strand doubling morphisms [MATH] and [MATH] with [MATH], where [MATH] is a subgroup of [MATH] of outer classes of inertia-preserving automorphisms of [MATH].
tldr: This paper interprets the Grothendieck-Teichmüller group as stabilizers of outer Lie algebra morphisms related to braid Lie algebras.
motivation: To provide a new algebraic interpretation of the Grothendieck-Teichmüller group using Lie algebras of infinitesimal braids.
method: The authors consider the action of outer automorphism groups on outer Lie algebra morphisms and show that the Grothendieck-Teichmüller group arises as the joint intersection of stabilizer groups of certain strand doubling morphisms.
result: The Grothendieck-Teichmüller group is expressed as the joint intersection of stabilizer groups of outer classes of strand doubling morphisms with a subgroup of inertia-preserving automorphisms.
conclusion: This offers a stabilizer interpretation of the Grothendieck-Teichmüller group in terms of braid Lie algebras.

title: An Extension Of A Theorem Of Chevet
authors: Fabien Souli Olivier Gu\'edon (LAMA)
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We adopt a modern approach to extend a comparison inequality of Chevet for Gaussian processes to a broader class of functions. Furthermore, we consider centered Gaussian random vectors associated with a family of [MATH] vectors on the unit sphere [MATH] and investigate configurations of the vertices for which these new functionals could be maximum for the regular simplex.
tldr: This paper extends a comparison inequality for Gaussian processes to a broader class of functions and studies configurations of vectors on the unit sphere.
motivation: To generalize Chevet's inequality for Gaussian processes and understand extremal configurations of spherical vectors.
method: Adopts a modern approach to extend the inequality and analyzes Gaussian random vectors on the sphere.
result: Provides an extension of Chevet's theorem and identifies conditions for the regular simplex to maximize certain functionals.
conclusion: The results contribute to geometric functional analysis and probability theory, but have no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Seed For Privacy -- Semi-automatic Privacy-revealing Data Reminder In Databases And Data Streams
authors: He Gu, Thomas Plagemann, Vera Goebel
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sharing databases and data streams imposes the danger of revealing private information in the form of complex events which can comprise individual data elements and their combinations. Identifying these privacy-revealing complex events is crucial for preserving privacy while maintaining data utility. However, data producers often lack the expertise to comprehensively identify these events, which undermines many state-of-the-art privacy-preserving mechanisms that rely on accurate event labeling. To address this challenge, we developed pArborist - a tool that can semi-automatically create a set of queries to identify and label privacy-revealing complex events in both static datasets and dynamic data streams, guided by the privacy requirements of the data producer. pArborist uses the schema of the database or data stream combined with initial input from the data producer, i.e., seed queries. From each seed query, pArborist grows a tree containing all possible syntactically correct queries, constrained by an upper limit on computational resources. Following this growing phase, the tree is refined by eliminating queries that lack correlation to the seed or are conditionally independent of the seed. Our evaluation indicates that pArborist achieves overall recall of 90% and precision of 93% in finding privacy-revealing queries, and this significantly surpasses the state-of-the-art approach FQID. In data stream processing experiments, pArborist introduces a delay of approximately 1.3 ms following an average warm-up period of 920 ms. The experiments also show that pArborist can automatically detect privacy-revealing complex events according to GDPR.
tldr: This paper presents a tool for semi-automatically identifying privacy-revealing complex events in databases and data streams.
motivation: Data producers often lack expertise to identify privacy-revealing events, undermining privacy-preserving mechanisms that rely on accurate event labeling.
method: The tool pArborist uses seed queries to grow a tree of syntactically correct queries, then refines it by eliminating uncorrelated or conditionally independent queries.
result: pArborist achieves 90% recall and 93% precision in finding privacy-revealing queries, surpassing the state-of-the-art FQID, with a delay of about 1.3 ms after warm-up.
conclusion: pArborist can automatically detect privacy-revealing complex events according to GDPR, aiding data producers in privacy protection.

title: Privacy-Preserving Intent Fulfilment And Assurance For 6g Ran
authors: Joss Armstrong
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intent-based network management is the emerging paradigm for 6G service lifecycle automation, with the 3GPP intent management framework (TS~28.312) defining creation, translation, fulfilment, and assurance stages. Existing fulfilment and assurance approaches require deep packet inspection, per-flow state tracking, or access to vendor-internal node telemetry to verify that provisioned resources satisfy expressed intents. These requirements conflict with regulatory constraints (GDPR, ePrivacy Directive) in multi-tenant networks and with vendor opacity in multi-vendor O-RAN deployments. We present an architecture for privacy-preserving intent fulfilment and assurance in which a coordinator provisions resources from declared intent categories without traffic inspection, and verifies fulfilment using only aggregate standardised PM counters at the O1 interface. A data-processing inequality argument shows that the resource allocation reveals at most [MATH] bits about traffic content, where [MATH] is the number of intent categories. We define two architectural privacy properties, intent-traffic unlinkability and node-opaque verification, and show that both hold by construction. Node-opacity does not sacrifice detection power: the aggregate verifier weakly dominates the per-agent verifier under a homogeneity condition. We map the architecture to the 3GPP intent lifecycle and the O-RAN Non-RT RIC, identifying the concrete interfaces, data objects, and deployment points at which the mechanism operates. On production PM counter data from four operator networks, increasing intent-category granularity sharpens provisioning but weakens assurance, consistent with the theoretical prediction that the privacy ceiling is a structural side effect of the detection constraint rather than a separate design parameter.
tldr: This paper proposes a privacy-preserving architecture for intent-based network management in 6G RAN, using aggregate counters to avoid traffic inspection.
motivation: Existing intent fulfilment and assurance methods require deep packet inspection or per-flow tracking, which conflict with privacy regulations and vendor opacity in multi-tenant and multi-vendor networks.
method: The architecture uses a coordinator that provisions resources based on declared intent categories without inspecting traffic, and verifies fulfilment using aggregate standardized PM counters at the O1 interface. A data-processing inequality argument bounds information leakage.
result: The architecture achieves intent-traffic unlinkability and node-opaque verification by construction, and the aggregate verifier weakly dominates per-agent verifier under homogeneity. Analysis on production data shows a trade-off between granularity and assurance.
conclusion: The paper demonstrates that privacy-preserving intent fulfilment and assurance is feasible without sacrificing detection power, and maps the architecture to 3GPP and O-RAN frameworks.

title: SLBench: Evaluating How Llm Agents Follow Logical Relations In Skills
authors: Xuan Chen, Chengpeng Wang, Lu Yan, Xiangyu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills extend LLM agents with reusable procedures, tools, and domain-specific workflows, but their safety depends on resolving dependencies among interacting instructions. We introduce SkillLogic, a framework for analyzing logical relations in skill files and constructing executable tests from them. Our taxonomy covers eight relation types, including preconditions that gate valid actions, constraints that limit how allowed actions may be performed, and fallbacks that specify recovery behavior after failure. Using SkillLogic, we scan over 5000 public skills and find that 70% contain at least one logical relation. We then construct SLBench, an 86-case executable benchmark from high-confidence, high-impact, and locally testable relations. Evaluating Codex and Claude Code across six LLM backbones shows unsafe rates up to 70%, with violations leading to privacy leaks, unsafe configuration changes, and incomplete cleanup. The human audit attributes failures to both agent capability gaps and low-salience skill text. We further show that SLGuard, a lightweight inference-time scaffold, reduces violations by 63% on targeted cases. Our results establish logical-relation following as a distinct reliability challenge for skill-guided agents.
tldr: This paper introduces SLBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents' ability to follow logical relations in skill files, and proposes SLGuard to reduce safety violations.
motivation: Agent skills often contain logical dependencies (preconditions, constraints, fallbacks) that LLM agents may fail to follow, leading to unsafe actions. There is a need to systematically evaluate and improve agents' adherence to these relations.
method: The authors develop SkillLogic, a framework to extract logical relations from skill files, and scan over 5000 public skills to build SLBench, an 86-case executable benchmark. They evaluate Codex and Claude Code across six LLM backbones and propose SLGuard, a lightweight inference-time scaffold.
result: Unsafe rates up to 70% are observed, with violations causing privacy leaks and unsafe changes. SLGuard reduces violations by 63% on targeted cases.
conclusion: Logical-relation following is a distinct reliability challenge for skill-guided agents, and inference-time scaffolds like SLGuard can mitigate risks.

title: Elusive But Coverable: The Recursion-Theoretic Structure Of Complete Abstract Interpretations
authors: Roberto Giacobazzi Nicklas Carpenter
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study local completeness and incompleteness of abstract interpretations from a recursion-theoretic perspective. Local completeness weakens global completeness and captures the absence of precision loss for a specific precondition: abstract computation yields exactly what is obtained by abstracting the corresponding concrete computation. This enables compositional reasoning and rules out false positives in verification. We characterize the distinction between static and dynamic program analysis in terms of uniformly decidable operations and observe that the latter is uniformly decidable only for trivial abstractions. We then prove that the class of programs inducing a predicate transformer that is locally complete for a given non-trivial abstract domain is elusive in a precise recursion-theoretic sense: it is a productive set, hence not computably enumerable, and, under mild hypotheses, the same holds for its complement. In particular, the first class lies in [MATH] and the second in [MATH]. Unlike the usual examples of [MATH] properties, we show that the classes of locally complete programs admit decidable coverings. This makes it possible to construct, via program transformation, an effective enumeration of a representative subset of programs that entirely covers this class -- capturing from the outside a class that eludes enumeration from within.
tldr: This paper studies local completeness and incompleteness of abstract interpretations from a recursion-theoretic perspective, focusing on program analysis rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The paper aims to characterize the precision loss in abstract interpretation and distinguish between static and dynamic program analysis using recursion-theoretic concepts.
method: The authors define local completeness and incompleteness, analyze uniform decidability, and prove that the class of programs inducing locally complete predicate transformers is productive and not computably enumerable.
result: They show that the class of locally complete programs is elusive (productive set) but admits decidable coverings, enabling effective enumeration of a representative subset.
conclusion: The work provides a recursion-theoretic characterization of completeness in abstract interpretation, with implications for program verification and analysis.

title: Blockchain-Linked Auditable Decision Management For Telecom/IoT Fraud-Control Requests
authors: Saviz Changizi, Nasibeh Mohammadzadeh, Mohammad Shojafar, Rahim Tafazolli
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09259v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Telecom fraud-control studies often stop at detector-level classification, but deployment use requires request-level policy resolution, lifecycle traceability, and auditability. This paper reframes fraud control as blockchain-linked auditable decision management for synthetic telecom/IoT fraud-control requests, and its main result is that the QLoRA-tuned LLM branch becomes much more usable than zero-shot prompting but mainly approaches, rather than outperforms, a lower-cost centralized ensemble. The framework maps each synthetic deployment record to a managed request, blocks explicit out-of-boundary cases through a deterministic hard-fraud gate, scores non-hard requests using centralized ML (M1), federated meta-learning (M2), or LLM-family risk sources (M3), and resolves actions through a shared five-state policy, two-zone refinement mechanism, and local Ethereum-compatible audit layer. Evaluation uses separate synthetic training data and a 100,000-record deployment replay corpus, so the study should be read as controlled drift-replay evidence rather than field validation or proof of live deployability. On validation, M1 gives the strongest balance, with legitimate-request FPR 0.0890 under the 0.10 operating cap and soft-fraud recall 0.8341. On labeled deployment replay, however, the legitimate-FPR gap becomes large: M1 rises to 0.1646 and M3-QLoRA to 0.1801, while M3-QLoRA reduces the M3-Base legitimate FPR from 0.3915 and reaches 0.8240 soft-fraud recall. Blockchain telemetry shows that lifecycle gas, cost, latency, and throughput differences are driven by submitted off-chain decision profiles rather than changes in fraud logic.
tldr: This paper proposes a blockchain-linked auditable decision management framework for telecom/IoT fraud control, using QLoRA-tuned LLMs and centralized ML models.
motivation: Telecom fraud-control studies often stop at detector-level classification, but deployment requires request-level policy resolution, lifecycle traceability, and auditability.
method: The framework maps synthetic deployment records to managed requests, uses a deterministic hard-fraud gate, and scores non-hard requests using centralized ML, federated meta-learning, or LLM-family risk sources, with actions resolved through a shared policy and Ethereum-compatible audit layer.
result: Centralized ML (M1) gives the strongest balance with legitimate-request FPR 0.0890 and soft-fraud recall 0.8341; QLoRA-tuned LLM reduces FPR but does not outperform M1.
conclusion: The framework provides controlled drift-replay evidence but is not field-validated; blockchain telemetry shows cost and latency differences driven by decision profiles rather than fraud logic.

title: AlphaZero In Sparsely Rewarded Games: Limits And Auxiliary Supervision
authors: Brent Kong, Tejas Ram, Tony Yue Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08984v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AlphaZero has demonstrated that a neural-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search can achieve superhuman performance, but strong play does not necessarily imply perfect play. We study this gap in two oracle-evaluable domains with contrasting structure: Connect Four, a solved partisan game with exact game-theoretic values, and Chomp, an impartial game whose optimal play is governed by Grundy-number structure. Under a unified self-play [MATH] MCTS pipeline, we compare vanilla AlphaZero, a multi-frame variant (limited to Chomp), and an AlphaZero Auxiliary Loss (AZAL) that adds oracle-derived policy supervision. We find that vanilla AlphaZero achieves strong play across both domains but cannot preserve the exact trajectories required for optimal play: in Connect Four, it fails to maintain the optimal line of play, while in Chomp, it fails to consistently restore the [MATH] invariant. On rectangular Chomp boards, multi-frame inputs alone do not remove this gap. Nevertheless, AZAL substantially improves oracle consistency across multi-seeded full-game traces and sampled-state evaluations. On Chomp, AZAL reaches perfect full-game oracle consistency on 10x11 and high but not complete consistency on 9x10; on Connect Four, AZAL improves oracle-match rate and delays the first oracle mistake, but does not reach perfect play.
tldr: This paper studies the limitations of AlphaZero in achieving perfect play in sparsely rewarded games like Connect Four and Chomp, and proposes an auxiliary loss to improve oracle consistency.
motivation: AlphaZero achieves superhuman performance but does not necessarily play perfectly; understanding this gap is important for AI safety and reliability.
method: The authors compare vanilla AlphaZero, a multi-frame variant, and an AlphaZero Auxiliary Loss (AZAL) that adds oracle-derived policy supervision on Connect Four and Chomp.
result: Vanilla AlphaZero fails to maintain optimal play trajectories; AZAL substantially improves oracle consistency but does not achieve perfect play on all boards.
conclusion: Auxiliary supervision can bridge the gap between strong and perfect play, but perfect play remains elusive for some game sizes.

title: A Formalization Of The Mean-Field Derivation Of The Vlasov Equation: AI-Assisted Lean Formalization As A Strategy Game
authors: Joseph K. Miller
abstract: ArXiv:2607.08986v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We formalize a research result in the Lean 4 proof assistant by having a mathematician direct an AI system, and frame the activity as a formalization game. The objective is to turn a LaTeX document into Lean. The game is won when the development compiles, contains no sorry, and a machine check shows the target theorems rest on Lean's foundational axioms alone. Reuse is a second check, by a definition we introduce: whether the development yields a self-contained layer of general mathematics the wider library could absorb. The case study is a complete, axiom-clean formalization of well-posedness for the nonlinear Vlasov equation via Dobrushin's mean-field route -- existence, uniqueness, the stability estimate and mean-field limit, and a short-window superposition principle (weak solutions are Lagrangian). The human's role was to direct, not to write proofs: to scope the definitions, steer the decompositions, and triage the library's gaps; the AI agent executed. The formalization certifies the proof of each statement as written; whether the written statement is the intended theorem stays the mathematician's judgment. The optimal-transport machinery that fell out of the build (in particular, properties of the Wasserstein-1 metric and the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality theorem) separates into a self-contained layer that compiles against Mathlib alone: about a sixth of the development (49 of 299 declarations), behind a 22-declaration interface with no reverse dependency. The headline theorems ran in about a week, the full development in about a month. We report the quantitative claims as observations of one game, not as general laws. The game's rules name no particular system, so the methodological framing is meant to outlast the tools of any one run.
tldr: This paper formalizes the mean-field derivation of the Vlasov equation in Lean 4 using AI assistance, framing the process as a strategy game.
motivation: The authors aim to demonstrate a methodology for formalizing mathematical proofs by combining human direction with AI execution, using a case study from kinetic theory.
method: A mathematician directs an AI system to convert a LaTeX document into Lean 4 code, with the goal of a complete, axiom-clean formalization of well-posedness for the nonlinear Vlasov equation via Dobrushin's mean-field route.
result: The formalization compiles without errors, contains no 'sorry', and includes a self-contained layer of optimal transport machinery (Wasserstein-1 metric, Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality) that compiles against Mathlib alone.
conclusion: The approach successfully formalizes a nontrivial mathematical result, but the paper's focus is on the formalization methodology rather than advancing quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Event Burst Trigger: An Availability Backdoor Attack On Event-Based Snn Object Detection
authors: Jaesun Baek, Chanwook Lee, Eun-Kyu Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2607.09115v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Event-based vision and spiking neural networks (SNNs) are increasingly adopted for edge intelligence under strict latency and energy constraints. However, the vulnerability of event-based SNN object detection models to availability backdoor attacks remains insufficiently studied. This paper presents Event Burst Trigger (EBT), an availability backdoor attack targeting SNN-based object detection models. EBT injects carefully crafted event-based triggers into the training data, which induce temporally concentrated event streams during inference. These burst-like activations increase the number of phantom (i.e., spurious) object candidates, and consequently inflate the computational cost of the post-processing stage, particularly Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS). We evaluate EBT on SpikeYOLO, the state-of-the-art SNN-based object detector, under a poison-only threat model that does not require modifications to the model architecture, loss function, or inference pipeline. Experimental results show that while detection accuracy remains largely preserved, with mAP@0.5 decreasing by less than 0.099, the latency of the NMS stage increases by up to 38%. This indicates that NMS can become a dominant availability bottleneck in event-based SNN object detection. Experiments on an edge platform further show that the proposed attack elevates baseline resource utilization and reduces scheduling slack without inducing conspicuous peaks in resource usage. In addition, STRIP-based backdoor detection fails to reliably distinguish the proposed attack from benign inputs. These results characterize a previously underexplored availability backdoor threat in event-based SNN object detection systems.
tldr: This paper presents an availability backdoor attack on event-based SNN object detection models, focusing on computational cost rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The vulnerability of event-based SNN object detection to availability backdoor attacks is insufficiently studied.
method: The authors inject crafted event-based triggers into training data to induce burst-like activations that increase phantom object candidates and inflate NMS computational cost.
result: Detection accuracy is largely preserved (mAP@0.5 drop <0.099) while NMS latency increases by up to 38%, and STRIP-based detection fails to distinguish the attack.
conclusion: This characterizes a previously underexplored availability backdoor threat in event-based SNN object detection systems.

method: The authors employ positron annihilation spectroscopy to probe atomic-scale defects and infer SRO structures in MPEAs.
result: The technique successfully identifies different SRO structures and correlates them with alloy composition and processing conditions.
conclusion: Positron annihilation spectroscopy is a viable tool for SRO characterization, offering insights for tailoring alloy properties.

title: Vibrational-Entropy-Driven Compensation Mechanism On The Rutile ${\mathrm{TiO}}_{2}\text{ }(111)$ Polar Surface

abstract:

Polar surfaces, known for their unique electronic and chemical properties, play vital roles in catalysis and electronics, yet their atomic structures remain difficult to resolve due to intrinsic instability often mitigated by surface reconstruction. However, the role of entropy, particularly vibrati…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 026201] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies vibrational entropy-driven compensation on a rutile TiO2 polar surface, a condensed matter physics topic unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Polar surfaces are important in catalysis and electronics but their atomic structures are hard to resolve due to instability; the role of entropy in stabilization is unclear.
method: The authors combine experimental techniques and theoretical calculations to investigate the atomic structure and vibrational entropy contribution on the rutile TiO2 (111) polar surface.
result: They identify a compensation mechanism driven by vibrational entropy that stabilizes the polar surface.
conclusion: Vibrational entropy plays a key role in stabilizing polar surfaces, which has implications for understanding surface properties in materials science.

title: Gravitational-Wave Tomography Of The Moon: Constraining Lunar Structure With Calibrated Gravitational Waves
authors: Han Yan And Jan Harms
abstract:
Author(s): Han Yan and Jan Harms

A proposed gravitational-wave observatory on the Moon might gather more information than previously thought, thanks to geology.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 021409] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes using a lunar gravitational-wave observatory to study the Moon's internal structure via seismic tomography.
motivation: Understanding the Moon's internal structure is important for planetary science, and gravitational-wave detectors on the Moon could provide new data.
method: The authors analyze how gravitational waves interact with the Moon's interior and propose a tomographic inversion technique to infer lunar structure from observed signals.
result: They show that a calibrated gravitational-wave observatory on the Moon can resolve subsurface features with improved resolution compared to traditional seismic methods.
conclusion: Lunar gravitational-wave observatories could serve dual purposes: detecting astrophysical gravitational waves and probing the Moon's interior.

authors: Kirill V. Bazarov And Oleg I. Tolstikhin
abstract:

It was shown that in rescattering photoelectron spectroscopy of chiral molecules, the enantiosensitive signal splits into two stage-resolved contributions from tunneling and rescattering. They can be controlled independently by varying the relative phase of an orthogonal two-color field.


[Phys. Rev. A 114, L011101] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies enantiosensitivity in rescattering photoelectron spectroscopy of chiral molecules using orthogonal two-color fields.
motivation: Understanding the mechanisms of enantiosensitivity in photoelectron spectroscopy can help distinguish chiral molecules, which is important in chemistry and biology.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the rescattering photoelectron spectroscopy signal and decompose it into contributions from tunneling and rescattering stages, controlled by the relative phase of an orthogonal two-color field.
result: The enantiosensitive signal splits into two stage-resolved contributions that can be independently controlled.
conclusion: This work provides a way to control enantiosensitivity in photoelectron spectroscopy, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Weak Decay Of The Positronium Ion
authors: Nishat Ul Sani, Muhammad Jamil Aslam, And Ishtiaq Ahmed
abstract:

The positronium ion [MATH], a Coulombic three-body bound state of two electrons and a positron, predominantly decays via electron-positron annihilation into electromagnetic final states. While its radiative decay channels have been extensively studied, much less attention has been giv…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012807] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the weak decay of the positronium ion, a three-body bound state, which is a topic in particle physics.
motivation: The weak decay channels of the positronium ion have received little attention compared to radiative decays, and understanding them could provide insights into fundamental interactions.
method: The authors perform theoretical calculations of the weak decay rate using quantum electrodynamics and weak interaction theory.
result: They compute the branching ratio for weak decay and find it to be extremely small compared to the dominant annihilation channel.
conclusion: The weak decay of the positronium ion is negligible for practical purposes, but the study confirms theoretical predictions and highlights the dominance of electromagnetic processes.

title: Odd-even High-order Harmonic Generation As A Symmetry-resolved Probe Of Intrinsic Molecular Asymmetry: From Spectra To Subcycle Interferometry
authors: Kim-Ngan H. Nguyen, Thanh Tran, Doan-An Trieu, Duong D. Hoang-Trong, Cam-Tu Le, Lan Nguyen Tran, Van-Hoang Le, And Ngoc-Loan Phan

method: The authors theoretically analyze odd-even HHG from oriented polar molecules, extracting amplitude-phase observables from spectral measurements.
result: They identify a complete set of observables connecting spectral measurements to microscopic emission dynamics.
conclusion: Odd-even HHG can serve as a symmetry-resolved probe of intrinsic molecular asymmetry.

result: The phase diagram shows the stability regions of various Ta2O5 polymorphs under different conditions.
conclusion: The study provides a theoretical phase diagram that can guide synthesis and application of Ta2O5.

[Phys. Rev. B 114, 034414] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.

motivation: The magnetic nature of RuO2 is under debate; recent experiments show it is a paramagnetic metal, but further characterization is needed.
method: Magnetic susceptibility and electrical resistivity measurements were performed on high-quality single crystals of RuO2.
result: The susceptibility shows a characteristic temperature dependence consistent with Fermi-liquid theory, and the resistivity follows a T^2 law.
conclusion: RuO2 exhibits conventional Fermi-liquid behavior, supporting its classification as a paramagnetic metal rather than an altermagnet.

method: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and density functional theory (DFT) calculations were used to study the electronic structure of TiSe2.
result: A surface resonance emerges from the CDW symmetry breaking, distinct from bulk states.
conclusion: Surface CDW symmetry breaking can induce new electronic states, offering insights into manipulating correlations and dimensionality at surfaces.

While prior studies have mainly focused on hyperbolic eigenmodes, the behavior of antihyperbolic surfa…

tldr: This paper studies antihyperbolic surface waves on twisted bilayer hyperbolic metasurfaces, focusing on topological reconfiguration and wave-front engineering.
motivation: To explore the behavior of antihyperbolic surface waves, which have been less studied than hyperbolic eigenmodes, and to demonstrate topological reconfiguration via rotational stacking.

result: They find that antihyperbolic surface waves exhibit unique directional canalization and can be reconfigured topologically by twisting the layers.
conclusion: Twisted bilayer hyperbolic metasurfaces provide a platform for flexible control of surface waves, with potential applications in wave-front engineering and topological photonics.

title: First-principles Study Of Quasiparticle Band Structures And Exciton Binding Energies Of Zintl ${am}_{2}{x}_{2}$ ($A=\mathrm{Ca}$, Sr, Ba; $M=\mathrm{Zn}$, Cd; $X=\mathrm{N}$, P, As, Sb) Solar Absorbers

method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory (GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation) are used to compute quasiparticle band structures and exciton binding energies.
result: The study provides detailed band structures and exciton binding energies for a series of Zintl compounds, identifying promising candidates for solar absorbers.
conclusion: These Zintl compounds show suitable electronic and optical properties for photovoltaic applications, warranting further experimental exploration.

motivation: Attaining a reliable complete basis set (CBS) limit remains a significant challenge in ab initio correlated electronic-structure calculations.
method: The authors extend their previous finite-element Delta-Sternheimer approach from atoms and diatomic molecules to polyatomic molecules, enabling numerically accurate random-phase approximation (RPA) correlation energies.
result: The method achieves accurate all-electron RPA correlation energies for polyatomic molecules, approaching the CBS limit.
conclusion: The finite-element Delta-Sternheimer approach is a promising technique for high-precision electronic structure calculations in molecules.

tldr: This paper studies charge carrier dynamics and photocatalytic properties of Janus PtSSe/BeP heterostructures for water splitting using first-principles calculations.
motivation: To explore two-dimensional heterostructures for efficient photocatalytic water splitting, a topic in materials science and renewable energy.
method: First-principles density functional theory (DFT) and nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations are employed to compute stability, electronic structure, optical properties, and charge transfer.
result: The SePtS/BeP and SPtSe/BeP heterostructures exhibit suitable band alignments and charge separation for water splitting.
conclusion: These heterostructures are promising photocatalysts for water splitting, but the work is purely computational materials science without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

tldr: This paper uses machine learning potentials to determine the melting phase relation of seifertite and pyrite-type SiO2 under high pressure.
motivation: The phase relations of high-pressure polymorphs of silica are poorly constrained, which is important for planetary science and industrial technology.
method: Two machine learning potentials (MLPs) for SiO2 were developed to faithfully represent the strongly anharmonic interactions and used to compute phase boundaries.
result: The MLPs accurately reproduce known phase boundaries and predict the melting curve of seifertite and pyrite-type SiO2.
conclusion: Machine learning potentials can effectively determine high-pressure phase relations of silica, providing insights into planetary interiors.

method: The author proposes a piecewise power-law model to describe subexponential growth dynamics and fits it to empirical data on word and name usage from online sources.

authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi
